publication.title: Flow Vision for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles via an Artificial Lateral Line
publication.publisher: EURASIP Journal on Advances in Signal Processing
publication.abstract: Most fish have the capability of sensing flows and nearby movements even in dark or murky conditions by using the lateral line organs. This enables them to perform a variety of underwater activities, such as localizing prey, avoiding predators, navigating in narrow spaces, and schooling. To emulate this capability for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles, we developed an artificial lateral line using an array of Micro-Electro-Mechanical-Systems (MEMS) flow sensors. The signals collected via the artificial lateral line are then processed by an adaptive beamforming algorithm developed from Capon’s method. The system produces 3D images of source locations for different hydrodynamic activities, including the vibration of a dipole source and the movement of a tailflicking crayfish. A self-calibration algorithm provides the capability of self-adaptation to different environments. Lastly, we give a Cramer-Rao bound on the theoretical performance limit which is consistent with experimental results.

Recovery of rectified signals from hot-wire/film anemometers due to flow reversal in oscillating flows
publication.abstract: Hot-wire/film anemometers have been broadly used in experimental studies in fluid mechanics, acoustics, and ocean engineering. Yet, it is well known that hot-wire/film anemometers rectify the signal outputs due to the lack of sensitivity to flow direction. This main drawback, in turn, makes them less useful for diverse fluctuating flow measurements. To solve this issue, a rectification recovery method has been developed based on reconstruction of the Fourier series expansion in conjunction with signal-squaring approach. This signal recovery method was experimentally examined and proven to be successful for both conventional and microfabricated hot-wire/film anemometers. The method was further applied to dipole field measurements, with data from recovered signals perfectly matching the analytical model of the dipole field.

Generation of flow tones due to flow past a deep cavity: effect of streamwise length
publication.abstract: Shear flow past a deep cavity can generate self-sustained oscillations, including locked-on flow tones, due to coupling between the inherent instability of the separated shear layer and an acoustic mode of the cavity resonator. This investigation focuses on the dimensionless pressure amplitude response with in a deep cavity, as a function of the streamwise length of the cavity opening; for each length, the pressure response is characterized over a wide range of dimensionless inflow velocity. Criteria for locked-on flow tones are assessed. They include a measure of the strength of lock-on, SoL and the quality factor Q. All self-excited oscillations are assessed using both of these criteria, in order to interpret dimensionless forms of the fluctuation pressure amplitude. The dimensionless pressure amplitude response of the cavity involves several successive regimes, due to variations of streamwise length L of the cavity opening. These regimes are defined in relation to L/y, where y is the momentum thickness of the inflow boundary layer. Below a minimum value of L/y, flow tones cannot be generated. Furthermore, these regimes are defined in terms of the possible hydrodynamic modes (stages) of the unsteady shear layer and the acoustic modes of the deep cavity.

Biomimetic flow imaging with an artificial fish lateral line
publication.publisher: Proceedings of BIOSIGNALS 2008 – International Conference on Bio-inspired Systems and Signal Processing
publication.abstract: Almost all fish possess a flow-sensing system along their body called the lateral line, which allows them to perform various behaviors such as schooling, preying, and obstacle or predator avoidance. Inspired from this, our group has built artificial lateral lines from newly-developed flow sensors using Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) technology. To make our lateral line a functional sensory system, we develop an adaptive beamforming algorithm (applying Capon’s method) that provides our lateral line with the capability of imaging the locations of oscillating dipoles in a 3D underwater environment. To help our sensor arrays adapt to the environment for better performance, we introduce a self-calibration algorithm that significantly improves the image accuracy. Finally, we derive the Cramer-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB) that represents the fundamental performance limit of our system and provides guidance in optimizing artificial lateral-line systems.

Simple Device for Electromagnetic Interference Shielding Effectiveness Measurement. IEEE Transactions on Electromagnetic Compatibility Practical Papers, Articles and Application Notes
publication.abstract: Abstract—The design, construction, and testing results of a simple flanged coaxial electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding effectiveness (SE) tester are presented in this paper. This tester is a coaxial holder with uniform diameters that maintain 50 Ohm impedance throughout the length of the device. The ends of the tester are designed to directly attach1 0 dB, 50 Ohm, attenuators with standard N-type connectors, which allow practical coupling of the device for installation and measurements. This device was primarily designed to overcome several shortcomings of the ASTM D4935-99 standard SE tester that besides having a relatively complex shape requires relatively large sample specimens for testing. Compared to the frequency band of operation, up to 1.5 GHz, of the ASTM D4935-99 standard coaxial EMI tester, the newly developed SE tester operates in a broader frequency range, theoretically up to 18.2 GHz. The tester was calibrated and the SE of common and new materials was determined through several experiments. The SE results were validated with expected theoretical outcomes.

publication.title: Biomimetic flow sensing using artificial lateral lines
publication.title_secondary: Volume 8: Heat Transfer, Fluid Flows, and Thermal Systems, Parts A and B
publication.abstract: By mimicking fish lateral lines and fish sensing behaviors, we constructed an artificial lateral line and employed it for biomimetic flow sensing. Thirteen hot-film anemometers were mounted to the surface of a NACA0015 airfoil to constitute the artificial lateral line. The resulting fish-like platform was maneuvered by a 3-degree-of-freedom robotic arm for two-dimensional mobility in aquatic environments. Assisted with specially developed algorithms, two biologically relevant flow sensing scenarios have been realized. They were tracking a nearby dipole source in still water by detecting the dipole flow field and tracking a distant stationary source in running water by detecting its hydrodynamic wake.

publication.title: Biomimetic imaging of flow phenomena
publication.title_secondary: 2007 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing - ICASSP '07
publication.publisher: Proceedings of the 32nd international Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
publication.abstract: Biologists have reported that fish form sensory maps to assist in the imaging of flow disturbances underwater, including those created by predator or prey, using the lateral-line flow-sensing system. Our group has invented artificial lateral-line systems based on both micromachined and commercial hot-wire anemometer sensors. In this paper, we report on the successful application of adaptive beamforming (Capon's method), in conjunction with an artificial lateral line, to visualize flow disturbances, including acoustic dipoles, underwater. Our preliminary results showcase, for the first time, an ability to image an entire region underwater using micro and millimeter scale arrays, thereby mimicking the flow- imaging abilities of fish.

Design and characterization of artificial haircell sensor for flow sensing with ultrahigh velocity and angular sensitivity
publication.abstract: We report the development of an artificial haircell (AHC) sensor with design inspired by biological haircells. The sensor consists of a silicon cantilever beam with a high-aspect-ratio cilium attached at the distal end. Sensing is based on silicon piezoresistive strain gauge at the base of the cantilever. The cilium is made of photodefinable SU-8 epoxy and can be up to 700-μm tall. In this paper, we focus on flow-sensing applications. We have characterized the performance of the AHC sensor both in water and in air. For underwater applications, we have characterized the sensor under two flow conditions: steady-state laminar flow (dc flow) and oscillatory flow (ac flow). The detection limit of the sensor under ac flow in water is experimentally established to be below 1 mm/s. A best case angular resolution of 2.16 degree is also achieved for the sensor’s yaw response in air.

Dielectric analysis of VGCNF reinforced polyethylene composites
publication.abstract: Dielectric analysis was performed on vapor grown carbon nanofiber reinforced high density polyethylene (HDPE) composites. The dielectric parameters (permittivity, loss factor, tan δ and ionic conductivity) of pure \HDPE\ and composites were obtained in a frequency range of 0.01–105 Hz and temperature range of 35–120 °C. The dielectric properties of pure \HDPE\ are slightly dependent on temperature and frequency. Permittivity values decreased slightly with frequency and temperature while changes in loss factor and dissipation factor (tan δ) were negligible. The dielectric properties of the composites showed a strong dependence on nanofiber content, testing frequency and temperature. Permittivity, loss factor and tan δ increased with the increase of nanofiber content and decreased with increasing temperature and frequency. Percolation phenomenon was observed in the dielectric analysis, similar to the percolation in electrical conductivity studies. The threshold value for permittivity and loss factor was ≈15 wt% VGCNF. The ionic conductivity of the composites increased with frequency.

publication.title: Effects of microwave assisted heating of carbon nanofiber reinforced high density polyethylene
publication.abstract: Carbon nanofiber and carbon nanotube reinforced polymer composites have shown promise due to their enhanced mechanical, electrical, thermal, and dielectric properties. In this study, vapor grown carbon nanofiber reinforced polyethylene composites were exposed to microwave radiation in a conventional resonance cavity microwave oven to explore the possibility of using microwave energy to assist the processing of carbon nanofiber reinforced thermoplastic composites and determine the effect of microwave radiation exposure on material properties. Average temperatures of up to 40 °C above ambient were measured after 5 min of microwave exposure. The effect of high power microwave radiation on the physical integrity of the composites via dynamic mechanical analysis, tensile tests, and dielectric analysis is presented. A drop of 50% in failure strain has been observed for composites with 15 and 20 wt% nanofiber concentrations after exposure to microwave radiation.

publication.abstract: We report the development and application of an artificial hair cell (AHC) flow sensor inspired by biological systems. With optimized design and fabrication process, the AHC is characterized in terms of sensitivity, calibration, and robustness. Especially, an AHC can discern variations of water flow down to 0.1mm/s and survive 55° deflections. The sensor has been applied to flow field measurements, matching perfectly with analytical and previous experimental results. By employing arrays of such AHC sensors, an artificial lateral line is constructed for biomimetic studies on localizing and tracking hydrodynamic events.

publication.title: TRAIL FOLLOWING OF TURBULENT WAKE USING ARTIFICIAL LATERAL LINE
publication.title_secondary: Proceeding of Fifth International Symposium on Turbulence and Shear Flow Phenomena
publication.abstract: Inspired by the unique flow imaging capability of fish lateral lines, we configured an artificial lateral line (ALL) in fish contour, and conducted biomimetic study on trail following of a hydrodynamic wake. The ALL consisted of 13 hot-film anemometers, and was integrated with a 3-degree of freedom robotic arm for movement in a 2-D plane. A circular cylinder was exposed in a water channel to generate the wake. Trail-following algorithm was developed based on wake characterization both numerically and experimentally, and was further optimized through applications of the ALL. We demonstrate that the robotic ALL can follow a wake successfully in various scenarios. Such efforts will lead to safer autonomous navigation of underwater vehicles in complex aquatic environment.

publication.title: Distant touch hydrodynamic imaging with an artificial lateral line
publication.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
publication.abstract: Nearly all underwater vehicles and surface ships today use sonar and vision for imaging and navigation. However, sonar and vision systems face various limitations, e.g., sonar blind zones, dark or murky environments, etc. Evolved over millions of years, fish use the lateral line, a distributed linear array of flow sensing organs, for underwater hydrodynamic imaging and information extraction. We demonstrate here a proof-of-concept artificial lateral line system. It enables a distant touch hydrodynamic imaging capability to critically augment sonar and vision systems. We show that the artificial lateral line can successfully perform dipole source localization and hydrodynamic wake detection. The development of the artificial lateral line is aimed at fundamentally enhancing human ability to detect, navigate, and survive in the underwater environment.

publication.title: Dynamic mechanical and thermal analysis of aligned vapor grown carbon nanofiber reinforced polyethylene
publication.abstract: Dynamic mechanical and thermal analysis of aligned vapor grown carbon-nanofibers (VGCNFs)-reinforced high-density polyethylene (HDPE) was performed. High-shear mixing was used to disperse and distribute the nanofibers. Extensional flow was used to obtain anisotropic nanoreinforced composite tapes. Dynamic mechanical analysis showed dual increase of storage modulus and loss modulus with different draw ratios. The modulus and complex viscosities of the drawn samples converged to that of pure PE at high temperatures, indicating that in the melt, the behavior is dominated by the semicrystalline matrix. Additionally, an increase in thermal stability was observed for the composites compared to PE matrix. Differential scanning calorimetry analysis showed that the inclusion of nanofibers hindered the structure evolution of PE upon drawing.

publication.title: Micromachined hot-wire boundary layer flow imaging array
publication.title_secondary: CANEUS2006: MNT for Aerospace Applications
publication.abstract: Boundary layer flow imaging can provide real time information for flight control of air vehicles, and collision avoidance and stealth detection of underwater vehicles. High density, micro-scaled sensor arrays based on microfabrication techniques have made it possible to enable these new applications. We report on the development of such a flow sensor array. It is realized by combining surface micromachining and three-dimensional assembly. It consists of a linear array of 16 integrated hot-wire anemometers (HWA) evenly spaced 1 mm apart. Each sensor uses a 400 μm long thermal element (hot-wire) that is made of a thin film nickel/polyimide composite, and is elevated 600 μm above the substrate. Under constant temperature (CT) mode, the threshold velocity sensitivity to water flow is down to 100 μm/s, and the frequency response to dynamic signals is up to 1000 Hz. The capabilities of the sensor array on boundary flow measurement and hydrodynamic wake imaging are demonstrated via wind tunnel and water channel experiments.

publication.title: Multi-layer embedment of conductive and non-conductive PDMS for all-elastomer MEMS
publication.publisher: Proceedings of the 12th International Conference on Solid-state Sensors, Actuators, and Microsystems
publication.abstract: PDMS (polydimethylsiloxane) elastomer is widely used in MEMS. However, PDMS is non-conductive and as a result is used in mostly structural applications. We report methods for monolithic integration of conductive and non-conductive PDMS for realizing wholly polymer-based devices with embedded elastomer wires, electrodes, heaters, and sensors. In this work we demonstrate elastomer strain gauges, capacitive pressure sensors, as well as microfluidic channels with integrated heaters and sensors. The process uses a series of PDMS patterning, micromolding, and bonding techniques with conductive PDMS features made by mixing with multiwall carbon nanotubes (MWNT).

publication.title: Multisensor processing algorithms for underwater dipole localization and tracking using MEMS artificial lateral line sensors
publication.publisher: EURASIP Journal on Advances in Signal Processing
publication.abstract: An engineered artificial lateral-line system has been recently developed, consisting of a 16-element array of finely spaced MEMS hot-wire flow sensors. This represents a new class of underwater flow sensing instruments and necessitates the development of rapid, efficient, and robust signal processing algorithms. In this paper, we report on the development and implementation of a set of algorithms that assist in the localization and tracking of vibrational dipole sources underwater. Using these algorithms, accurate tracking of the trajectory of a moving dipole source has been demonstrated successfully.

publication.title: Polymer micro and nano scale fabrication technology development for bioinspired sensing
publication.title_secondary: 2006 1st IEEE International Conference on Nano/Micro Engineered and Molecular Systems
publication.abstract: We report on the development of new elastomers and processes that utilize polymers such as PDMS, FSR (force sensitive resistor) polymer, MWCNT, and polyurethane to realize bioinspired sensors such as artificial haircells. In nature, haircell sensors are used by fish to sense flow, by spiders to sense vibration, and by some vertebrates for hearing and acoustics. An artificial haircell sensor is designed to mimic the ability of natural haircells to sense flow, vibration, and touch. However, in order to improve the sensitivity and robustness, the use of polymers is necessary. In this paper, we present the different generations of bioinspired artificial haircell sensors, along with the polymers and processes needed for their construction.

publication.title: Interaction of a deep water wave with a vertical cylinder: flow structure and loading
publication.abstract: Interaction of a deep-water wave with a vertical cylinder is characterized using techniques of high-image-density particle image velocimetry, in conjunction with measurement of the transverse and in-line loading coefficients. Phase-locked patterns of locally two-dimensional vortex formation are attainable only for sufficiently high values of the Keulegan–Carpenter number KC, e.g. KC>=12. Even in these cases, such patterns are interrupted by non-phase-locked patterns that, nevertheless, show basic forms, including mode inversion or switching of the initially formed vortex from the cylinder, along with patterns of symmetrical vortex formation, all represented by patterns of instantaneous vorticity. Three-dimensionality of the flow structure along the span of the cylinder shows, at relatively low KC, patterns of transverse velocity v and streamwise vorticity ωx that have well-defined spanwise spacing. This spacing decreases in a continuous fashion with depth beneath the free surface, and is in accord with the decrease of local KC with depth, i.e. decrease of the diameter of the local particle trajectory. Such three-dimensional patterns are, however, not phase repetitive over a large number of wave cycles. At sufficiently high values of KC, it is possible to identify basic classes of three-dimensional patterns. When regions of transverse velocity show like sign over a significant spanwise extent of the cylinder, the transverse loading coefficient is relatively large. As the number of zero crossings between the positive and negative regions of v increases, the transverse loading coefficient decreases accordingly. Generally speaking, at these higher values of KC, patterns of streamwise vorticity are much less ordered, and of smaller scale; they are embedded within larger-scale well-defined patterns of the transverse velocity v along the span. Taken together, the patterns of locally two-dimensional (sectional) structure and the three-dimensional structure along the span indicate a criterion for locally phase-locked quasi-two-dimensional vortex formation: it occurs when the pattern of transverse velocity is of the same sign over a significant spanwise distance along the span of the cylinder.

publication.title: Quantitative imaging of flow-structure interactions: origin of unsteady loading and vibration
publication.publisher: Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Flow-Induced Vibrations
publication.abstract: In recent decades, substantial insight has been gained into the origin of unsteady loading of bodies via pointwise measurements of flow parameters and pressure away from, and at, the surface of the body, as well as measurements of the overall loading. As a complement, wholefield imaging can provide quantitative interpretations of the flow structure away from and immediately adjacent to the surface. These imaging approaches can yield global representations of: the flow topology including critical points; spectra and cross-spectra; orthogonal, phase-locked, as well as intermittent/ modulated, patterns of vorticity and velocity; and space-time volumes of these quantities. All of these approaches employ techniques of high-image-density particle image velocimetry. Selected case studies are described herein.

publication.abstract: We present a new approach to simulating wave–structure interaction dynamics using proper orthogonal decomposition by directly employing eigenmodes extracted from particle image velocimetry experimental data. A low-dimensional Galerkin model is constructed incorporating up to 12 modes and time-dependent boundary conditions. A penalty method is introduced to deal effectively with such boundary conditions. Our results suggest that this model represents accurately the flow dynamics, and it is asymptotically stable without the use of any ad hoc dissipation or other stabilization schemes. Our findings are documented by applying this approach to studying the vorticity dynamics of wave–cylinder interactions at Keulegan–Carpenter numbers of 9.3 and 13.9.

publication.title: Flow past two cylinders in tandem: instantaneous and averaged flow structure
publication.abstract: A technique of high-image-density particle image velocimetry is employed to characterize the instantaneous and averaged patterns of velocity, vorticity and Reynolds stress due to flow past two cylinders in tandem. These features of the flow patterns are characterized in the gap region as a function of the distance between the cylinders. In turn, they are related to the patterns in the near-wake of the two-cylinder system. Along the gap between the cylinders, small-scale concentrations of vorticity are formed in the separated shear layers. These concentrations buffet the surface boundary layer on the downstream cylinder, and thereby influence the eventual shedding of large-scale vortices. Within the gap, the instantaneous structure of the recirculation zones can exhibit both symmetrical and asymmetrical patterns. In the near-wake of the downstream cylinder, the form of the vortex shedding, as well as the averaged patterns of the flow structure, are substantially altered, relative to the case of a single cylinder. The width of the near-wake, as represented by averaged patterns of vorticity, is substantially narrower and the magnitudes of the peak Reynolds stress are significantly attenuated. On the other hand, if the gap region is sufficiently large such that Karman-like vortices form between the cylinders, the near-wake of the downstream cylinder shows distinctive patterns, and both the wake width and the magnitude of the Reynolds stresses become larger, relative to those at smaller gap width.

publication.title: Wave interaction with a vertical cylinder: spanwise flow patterns and loading
publication.abstract: A vertical cylinder is located in a free-surface wave, and a two-camera version of high-image-density particle image velocimetry is employed to characterize the spanwise modes of the flow structure in terms of instantaneous velocity and vorticity. These modes are classified according to organized patterns of velocity in the near wake, and are further interpreted in terms of distinctive arrangements of streamwise vorticity concentrations. At low Keulegan–Carpenter number, which corresponds to small wave height, locally two-dimensional vortices having small scale and circulation tend to form as a symmetrical pair and remain attached, or in close proximity, to the surface of the cylinder. Along the span of the cylinder, the near wake shows either a sinuous S or a unidirectional U mode. The spanwise wavelength λ of the S modes, relative to the cylinder diameter D, lies in the range 1 [less, similar] λ/D [less, similar] 4:5. These values of λ/D represent the spacing between extrema of patterns of cross flow velocity, as well as between clusters of streamwise vorticity of like sign. As the free surface is approached, the value of λ/D scales with the ratio of the minor to major axes of the elliptical particle trajectory of the wave. At moderate values of the Keulegan–Carpenter number, locally two-dimensional vortices having large scale and circulation are shed from the cylinder in an asymmetric arrangement. The corresponding spanwise mode represents the phase variation of this shedding along the span of the cylinder. These sinuous S modes involve large-scale distortions of patterns of both cross flow velocity and streamwise vorticity, which have wavelengths in the range 10 [less, similar] λ/D[less, similar] 110, in contrast to the spacing between individual concentrations of vorticity, which is 1:5D to 4D. Remarkably, it is possible to attain a unidirectional U mode, whereby the phase of the locally two-dimensional vortex shedding is preserved along the entire extent of the cylinder. Signatures of the moments due to the transverse and in-line forces on the cylinder were acquired simultaneously with the patterns of instantaneous velocity and vorticity. Severe modulations of the moment due to the transverse force are associated with spontaneous transformations between basic forms of the sinuous S and unidirectional U modes. The overall form of the signature of the moment due to the in-line force is, however, not generally affected by the spontaneous transformation between modes, but distortion of its peaks is evident.

Acquisition of a GPU-Enhanced Advanced Computing and Simulation Instrumentation for Interdisciplinary AI Research and Education at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: (The proposal was a preproposal submitted to UTRGV for an internal competition.) As UTRGV researchers address critical problems across divers fields that demand the analysis and management of complex, data-intensive problems, the university faces an increasing demand for high-performance computing (HPC) resources to effectively train modern AI models and conduct large-scale simulations. While some HPC resources are available both on and campus, limitations such as long job queues, insufficient graphics processing unit (GPU) memory, and slow interconnects often delay study results by days or force researchers to transfer sensitive data to remote supercomputer facilities. Moreover, while modern large language models (LLMs) are in high demand at UTRGV for a range of applications, existing cloud solutions are costly and pose privacy concerns. To address this gap, the proposal seeks funding to acquire a GPU-Enhanced Advanced Computing and Simulation Instrumentation (GACSI) equipped with the latest NVIDIA B200 GPUs. The B200 GPUs will enable UTRGV to deploy, fine-tune, evaluate, and operate LLMs entirely on campus, significantly reducing waiting times, eliminating cloud-based usage fees, and ensuring the privacy and security of sensitive data. Hosting these models locally will support the development of new hands-on course modules, allowing both undergraduate and graduate students to engage directly with state-of-the-art generative AI.

grant.title: Center of Excellence for Bi-regional Large Offshore Wind System (BLOWS)
grant.abstract: The mission of the proposed Center of Excellence for B i-regional L arge O ffshore W ind S ystem (BLOWS) is to conduct research and prepare future leaders in floating offshore wind energy, to serve as a technical hub, and to develop best practices and innovative solutions to promote offshore wind energy at Gulf of Mexico and Great Lakes regions. This work is proposed by a team of experts from four universities (The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, Illinois Institute of Technology, University of Houston, and Iowa State University), two national labs (Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Sandia National Lab), industry partners (TPI Composites, GE Vernova, ), and one technical authority in marine structures and systems (American Bureau of Shipping). The four institution members have a long history of performing research on marine engineering, renewable energy and advanced additive manufacturing science and technologies that support renewable energy. Our center differentiates itself by focusing on broadening geographic coverage to promote bi-regional collaboration. While many existing centers concentrate on regional or single-coast initiatives, our approach spans both the Great Lakes and Gulf of Mexico Coasts, which are not yet in the realm of geographic coverage of WETO, providing necessary research, technical support, and education programs tailored to solve unique atmospheric challenges in the two regions with a focus on floating offshore wind energy systems leveraging unique regional resources and expertise to drive innovation across diverse marine environments.

grant.title: Equipment: MRI: Track 1 Acquisition of Polytec MSA-600 Micro System Analyzer for Biomedical Engineering
grant.abstract: Requested Instrument: Polytec MSA-600-X/U Micro System Analyzer ($695,790), state-of-the-art instrument crucial for biomedical engineering research and education the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). The location of the instrument is the BIO-MEMS Laboratory (Director Caruntu). Servingover 34,000 students, UTRGV is a non-PhD-granting, minority-serving institution with a predominantly Hispanic student body (92%). The university aims to become an emerging research institution and establish a strong biomedical engineering community. This advanced equipment is crucial to preparing students in engineering, science, and medicine by providing hands-on research experiences that can lead to graduate studies, academic roles, or leadership positions in industry. UTRGV is experiencing rapid growth, with increasing student enrollment and the hiring of new faculty. A recently formed Biomedical Engineering(BME) Cluster for research and education includes eight faculty members, four of whom were hired within the past two years. Supporting faculty research development depends on access to cutting-edge infrastructure like the requested analyzer. Securing this grant lays a foundation for attracting external funding and fostering multidisciplinary collaborations. The lack of this instrument currently limits research efforts. This proposal is strongly supported by UTRGV administration, aligning with the university’s strategic goal of building a robust biomedical engineering research and education program.

Next Generation PTC-Integrated Onboard Smart Technologies and Training for Rolling Stock Condition Monitoring to Mitigate Train Derailment
grant.abstract: The Brotherhood of Railroad Signalmen (BRS) propose an initiative aimed at enhancing railway safety by proactively preventing train derailments caused by wheel and bearing failure through the deployment of new onboard sensors, PTC connectivity and workforce training and deployment. BRS (in partnership with a technology provider, a university railway center and a railway testing facility) will research, plan, and implement a workforce development strategy to deploy this new technology as a supplement to the current wayside Hot Box Detectors (HBDs). The technology will provide the ability for carriers to identify and detect a potential failure well in advance of a catastrophic failure while railcars are in service. This project centers on the application of wireless onboard sensors, which measure temperature, vibration, and other metrics of railcar bearings and wheels, to the railroad industry environment to enhance the safety and efficacy of railroad operations. Implementation of this technology, and communications with the railroad, with real-time data, will dramatically increase the level of safety currently available and further reduce and/or eliminate the risk of a failure causing an on-road derailment while enhancing condition-based maintenance practices.

grant.title: Ocean-based humidification-dehumidification desalination with self-sustainability
grant.abstract: An ocean-situated novel desalination technology is proposed. It employs a humidification-dehumidification (HDH) process to desalinate seawater. The process is completely and directly powered by nature, mainly by marine energy. Waves, tides, ocean currents, ocean thermal, and ocean salinity jointly function in a natural way to enable and maintain the HDH process. Winds and solar thermal further augment desalination production. The proposed research focuses on marine energy for HDH desalination. Wind and solar energy are auxiliary rather than necessary. Innovations of this HDH technology are reflected in both individual subsystems and the integrated overall system. The most innovative subsystems include a hydrokinetic heater and a humidifier. The hydrokinetic heater uses a hydro turbine to harvest hydrokinetic energy from water motion and directly convert it into heat, where the water motion can be caused by waves, tides, and/or ocean currents. The humidifier employs an array of wet cloth sheets to interact with passing-by hot and dry air for humidification, where the cloth wetting is maintained either by falling water films through wave overtopping or by natural wicking in lack of waves, and the salinity levels inside and outside the humidifier are balanced through natural diffusion. Upon integration of all the subsystems, the self-sustaining overall system is expected to produce freshwater in all weather conditions with zero electricity consumption (purely mechanical) and zero brine discharge (environmentally friendly). It will be a great fit for decentralized water supply at a low cost.

Effect of Long-Term Inactivity on Railcar Bearing Lubricant Performance
grant.sponsor: University Transfportation Center for Railway Safety
grant.sponsor_type: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: The performance of railroad bearings that sit idle in railyards, large industrial plants, or shipping ports has only recently been explored. Some of the bearings, with documented periods of inactivity exceeding 18 months, have been associated with major derailments. This provides a basis for concerns that the inactive periods contributed to early failure, possibly through degradation of the grease properties brought on by moisture intake or grease separation leading to uneven protection of the metal components. The proposed work builds on prior efforts conducted in collaboration with CSX Transportation and seeks to improve our understanding of the effects of long-term inactivity on lubricant properties. The proposed work would consist of (a) Preparation of test bearings which will be placed outdoors in a position to receive direct sunlight. (b) Placement of grease samples in the same location in a simulated bearing housing to mimic the thermal cycle of a sun-exposed bearing. (c) regular sampling from the simulated bearing housing to monitor long-term changes in lubricant performance and condition. (d) at intervals of 3 months, bearings will be removed and installed on a laboratory test rig and run for 1,000 simulated miles with continuous performance monitoring of temperature rise, vibration spectra, and power consumption, (e) post-test inspection including disassembly, teardown, and visual inspection of all bearing components, and (f) analysis of the grease composition at all stages with specific focus on loss of oxidation inhibitors and changes in tribological performance.

grant.title: Promoting Experiential Learning in STEM through Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences
Promoting Experiential Learning Through CUREs for Latinx Students
grant.abstract: Project Summary The CUREs@RGV proposal is being submitted for consideration to the Engaged Student Learning Track (Track 1) as a design, development, and research study that will investigate the effects of a course-based undergraduate research experience (CURE) on undergraduate student outcomes, including learning, academic achievement, as well as attitudes and interest in STEM. The first objective of this study is to provide professional development to STEM faculty (Biology, Biomedical, and Engineering) at UTRGV and STC to support their development and implementation of a CURE curriculum for undergraduate students. There is considerable evidence that CUREs improve student learning and interest in STEM. In addition, CUREs are an opportunity to provide more students with research experiences. The second objective of this study is to investigate faculty’s perceptions of undergraduate students’ abilities to engage in research and their self-efficacy toward designing and implementing CUREs. The third objective of this study will investigate the extent to which a CUREs laboratory affects (1) student learning outcomes and (2) attitudes/interest in STEM, as compared to learners experiencing a traditional lab. The fourth and final objective of this study is to strengthen the 2- to 4-year college pathway for STEM majors. Intellectual Merit To advance knowledge in STEM education and across STEM disciplines, we will draw from the literature on the development and implementation of CUREs (25, 47). Research demonstrates that CUREs improve students' achievement, retention, self-perceptions about learning, as well as scientific thinking and practices. The project team will support STEM faculty’s development of CUREs through a year-long professional development that includes development, implementation, and evaluation. The team will study the effects of CUREs curriculum on students’ learning, attitudes and interest in STEM. CUREs@RGV aims to 1) generate empirical evidence that will advance our understanding of how to improve undergraduate engagement, interest, and learning in STEM through CUREs; 2) improve STEM faculty’s self-efficacy toward CUREs and perceptions toward their students; and 3) strengthen pathways for students who have been marginalized in STEM education and careers. Because of the uniqueness of UTRGV, the study will focus on undergraduates who have been historically marginalized and underrepresented in STEM careers. This study draws on experiential learning theories and empirical findings in the literature on course-based undergraduate research experiences. Broader Impacts CUREs@RGV will lead to societal benefits in the short- and long-term. In the short-term, the project investigates ways to address the learning needs of undergraduate students in STEM courses through faculty professional development. The project will provide students, predominantly Latinx, with undergraduate research experiences that will lead to improved engagement, interest, and learning in STEM. The project will directly impact 24 STEM faculty at UTRGV and STC and approximately 600 undergraduate students in their CUREs course. In addition, over the three years, the project will indirectly impact 45 STEM faculty that attend the annual STEM Education conference, which is organized by the PI. A workshop will be conducted by the project team and in collaboration with the STEM faculty who have successfully implemented a CURE in their course. However, the ultimate impact is much broader as the research will be disseminated nationally through STEM education conference and journal publications. As a result, the project will help to broaden participation of Latinx students in STEM. The uniqueness of the RGV population is that more than 90% of the community is Latinx, of which approximately 85% are of Mexican descent.

grant.title: REU SITE: Interdisciplinary Research Experience for Undergraduates in Materials Science and Engineering at UTRGV
grant.abstract: This REU Site award to the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) will support the training of diverse undergraduate students in cutting edge research for 10 weeks during the summers of 2025-2027. A total of 30 students will be supported by the REU site in a three-year comprehensive engineering research activity. The students will be exposed to hands-on learning experience in the basics of materials science and engineering, involved in cutting-edge multidisciplinary research activities with aim to enrich their skills in the interrelationship between structure-processing-properties and performance of materials and nano/biomaterials. Exposure to these engineering research frontiers will arouse the students’ interest in pursuing higher education and considerably help increase both the number of students who choose engineering as their careers andthe education standards of UG students from minority and underrepresented groups across the USA. The REU site will also expand the knowledge and understanding of the technical projects by the students to develop and use diverse materials in real applications. The impact of this project will be already broadened by the direct participation of a HSI in engineering (UTRGV) as well as enhancing and maintaining an engineering-going (and a college-going) culture in a Hispanic- concentrated population. The REU site will also change the stereotypical gender and race assumptions in engineering and STEM study and career choice, especially for underrepresented Hispanic and women students. The proposed research activities will benefit society and national interest by advancing the existing knowledge in materials science and engineering and supporting diversity, research, and education at the national level.

grant.title: Track 4 - Phase II: Center for Broadening Participation in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich, Examine (CBPE-E4)
Wave-induced omnidirectional flow interaction with a vertical-axis unidirectional rotor
grant.abstract: The proposed work focuses on wave-rotor interaction, where waves induce omnidirectional water flows in the proximity of ocean surfaces and drive a vertical-axis rotor for unidirectional rotation. The rotor is a key component of a wave turbine, the latter being an emerging wave energy converter (WEC) technology. Unlike well-established wind turbine aerodynamics that deals with wind turbine interaction with unidirectional flows (winds), very little is known about wave turbine hydrodynamics that deals with wave turbine interaction with omnidirectional flows (waves). The main objectives of this project are to: (i) fill the knowledge gap in wave-rotor interaction through experimental study and, (ii) nurture more research on wave turbine hydrodynamics using obtained results. Ocean waves carry a huge amount of renewable energy that is largely untapped. While there are a large variety of WEC technologies under exploration in industry and academia, the wave turbine concept demonstrates certain key advantages and great potential. Success of the project will not only advance the wave turbine technology but also contribute to the sustainable development of coastal regions globally. The project will involve both graduate and undergraduate minority students in research. It will also promote STEM education in a coastal, cross-border, and Hispanic community.

Effect of Climate-induced Extreme Temperature on Rail Network Safety
grant.abstract: Temperature is one of the major factors related to the buckling of railway tracks. Due to the increase in frequency and intensity of heat waves in recent years, there is a need to study the effect of climate-induced extreme temperature events on the vulnerability of the rail infrastructure to buckling. The proposed project aims to address that need with an interconnected methodology that combines structural analysis and network-level vulnerability assessment. The findings of this project are expected to support decision-making to allocate funds for rehabilitation projects of vulnerable tracks and new construction to support high-risk routes. The project will be performed by a team of researchers at the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). The proposed budget for the project is $100,000. The timeline is expected to require 11 months.

grant.title: ERI: Hydrodynamic and transport characteristics of water films falling down cloth substrates with grazing airflows
grant.abstract: The proposed work is on investigation of gravity-driven liquid falling films flowing over cloth substrates. The main goal is to gain fundamental knowledge on hydrodynamic and transport characteristics of the falling films that interact with passing by gas flows. In this type of two-phase flows, the falling films offer substantially enlarged contact aera and greatly lengthened contact time with the adjacent gas flows for effective heat and mass transfer. With nonporous and rigid substrates such as stainless-steel walls, falling films have very broad industrial applications and have been extensively studied over the years. With porous and flexible substrates such as cloths, on the other hand, very little knowledge has been gained. A novel application of the latter as proposed by the PI is to make seawater flow down vertical cloth sheets as thin films to humidify passing by airflows – a key process in humidification-dehumidification desalination. Other potential applications may include cooling of buildings, absorption of carbon dioxide, etc. Cloth substrates are very different in many ways from solid substrates, which will largely alter hydrodynamic and transport characteristics of the associated falling films. In this proposed project with focus on cloth substrates, we will conduct experimental research to: (i) identify such key differences, (ii) determine morphological evolution of the falling films, (iii) quantify the interfacial evaporation mass flux in correlation with the heat exchanging rate and, (iv) establish parametric interrelationships between hydrodynamic and transport characteristics. The project will provide an opportunity for minority students in all the levels from graduate to K-12 to participate in research in various ways.

grant.title: Faculty Seed Research Grant: Laser Surface Texturing based on FEA and CFD Simulations as an Innovative Technique for Addressing Multi-disciplinary Challenges in Engineering Applications
grant.sponsor_type: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: This study aims to utilize Laser Surface Texturing (LST) in combination with Finite Element Analysis (FEA) and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations to improve the performance and longevity of important components in three distinct fields: prosthetic materials, rolling-element bearings, and airfoils. The goal is to enhance the quality of life and industrial performance by increasing the efficiency of prosthetic materials and rolling-element bearings. In airfoils, LST is being explored as a method to reduce drag and improve aerodynamic efficiency. The study involves applying LST to these components and then extensively evaluating the effects through experimentation and computational modeling. The FEA and CFD simulations will provide detailed insights into the performance of the LST-treated surfaces under various operating conditions. The findings of this research project are expected to have significant implications for biomedical engineering, materials science, mechanical engineering, and aeronautics, paving the way for future development and optimization.

grant.title: Faculty Seed Research Grant: Wave powered autonomous underwater vehicle
grant.sponsor: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.sponsor_type: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: An autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) can fulfill various missions in the ocean. While most AUVs are powered by batteries, their endurances are limited from a few hours to a few days only. We propose a novel technology that can enable an AUV to harvest energy from its surroundings—the ocean waves—for self-recharging to greatly lengthen its endurance to a few months or even longer. The proposed concept AUV is in a torpedo shape and employs a fully hull-encapsulated mass-spring-damper system (i.e., a direct linear electric generator) as its power take-off (PTO) unit. While in the recharging mode, the AUV surfaces and converts wave energy for electricity. Considering the AUV of a common size on the order of 1 meter, resonance of the AUV and/or its PTO, to be excited by ocean waves, becomes impossible in typical ocean conditions. In this work, we will realize a medium-fidelity wave powered AUV model in a bench scale and test it in the PI’s wave tank. This medium-fidelity model will allow us to explore non-resonant methods and approaches to enhance the AUV’s capability on wave energy harvesting. The research findings will augment knowledge in wave energy conversion, AUV development, system dynamics, and wave-structure interaction. They will also support our future applications for external grants to advance our wave powered AUV research.

grant.title: National Security & Engineering Partnership (NSEP)
Strategies and Technologies for Warning, Detection, and Prevention of Trespassing in the Vicinity of Highway-Rail Grade Crossings: State of the Practice and Research Needs
grant.abstract: The U.S. rail network is the largest, safest, and most efficient rail network in the world that operates over 160,000 rail miles. It plays a pivotal role in enabling the transportation of goods and people throughout the nation; and due to this crucial function, it serves as a fundamental pillar in supporting the economic expansion of the United States (Federal Railroad Administration, 2023). Simultaneously, the U.S. highway network plays a crucial role in enabling the seamless transportation of both individuals and cargo, consisting of a sophisticated linked grid of roads that spans the entire nation. According to data from the U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT), the average monthly traffic volume for the year 2022 exceeded 3,000 billion miles. However, at the intersection of these two crucial transportation modes lies a point of concern—the Highway Rail Grade Crossing (HRGC). HRGCs are where a road or pathway intersects with a railway track. These crossings facilitate the safe passage of vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians across railway lines. However, if road users fail to notice warning signals and attempt to cross the tracks when a train is approaching, a catastrophic collision can occur, leading to severe injuries or fatalities. As such, HRGCs are a critical cause of hazardous conditions that may involve collisions between trains and vehicles or pedestrians. Thousands of highway-rail incidents occur in the US every year. Such incidents include many fatal crashes. Between 2010 and 2018, a total of 1,114 fatal crashes tragically occurred at HRGCs in the United States that resulted in the loss of 1,306 lives. Trespassing at-or-near HRGC is a major safety issue. Trespassers are most often pedestrians trying to take a shortcut and/or do not notice incoming trains. Although it is illegal, more than 400 rail trespass fatalities occur every year. Various technologies and practices have been proposed to detect trespassing at rail crossings. Such technologies can involve various types of sensors such as radar, laser, infrared, magnetic, and many others. Such technologies can be infrastructure-based, locomotive-based, or a combination of both. Some innovative technologies include CCTV cameras assisted by computer vision, depth-sensing cameras, stereo vision, laser systems, and smart sensors enabled by deep learning, among others. Naturally, various technologies and practices come with diverse considerations, including aspects like their reliability, cost-effectiveness, accuracy, and smooth integration into rail infrastructure systems. There is a need to explore the advantages and disadvantages of existing and emerging technologies considering the needs and challenges of the rail infrastructure. The outcomes of this exploratory investigation guide decision-making and future research to prevent trespassing at HRGCs and improve the safety of the U.S. rail network.

grant.title: Acquisition of Metal Additive Manufacturing Machine to Support Defense Manufacturing Research and Innovation at Rio Grande Valley and the National IDREAM4D Consortium
grant.sponsor: DoD U.S. Army Contracting Command – Aberdeen Proving Ground – Research Triangle Park Division
grant.abstract: Groundbreaking advances in advanced manufacturing processes and smart technologies for cyber-physical systems are driving revolutions in materials/structures design and synthesis, providing innovation opportunities that transform a broader spectrum of military systems where advanced performance and protection at extreme conditions are expected. The objective of this request is to support a stream of ongoing research projects and two national consortia led by the PI team, through which 4 minority institutions are supported. Specifically, this requested major equipment supports UTRGV DoD Consortium for Innovation Driven Research Education for Advanced Manufacturing for the Defense (I-DREAM4D, www.idream4d.org) funded by DoD ($3.9 million, 2020-2024). The consortium is composed of five higher education institution members with three minority-serving institutions (UTRGV, UTSA, and Virginia State University), two national labs (Army Research Lab, Oak Ridge National Lab), members from defense industry, local high schools, and community colleges. The requested metal additive manufacturing machine facilitates the goals of the consortium to 1) advance research in material engineering through additive manufacturing (AM) and AI; 2) sustain an innovation-driven manufacturing education ecosystem to prepare future scientists and engineers who lead U.S. defense manufacturing innovation; and 3) expose and recruit future STEM talents through high school summer manufacturing innovation camps , and regional defense expos/exhibitions planned in 5 regions the consortium serves with a total population of 20 million, most of which are from underrepresented minority groups. UTRVG, a multi-campus and the nation’s second-largest Hispanic-serving institute (HSI) has a record high total enrollment of 32,618 in Fall 2020, of whom 89.4% are Hispanic. The requested equipment is critical to the goal of increasing participation of underrepresented minorities in all STEM programs and specifically in advanced materials and manufacturing while broadening and enhancing UTRGV’s core priority of student success through engaged learning, research, and creative works that will transform the Rio Grande Valley, the Americas, and beyond. The requested Metal Additive Manufacturing Equipment supports funded research projects and education programs organized in three levels, with the participation of minority students and faculty at UTRGV: 1) Advanced material synthesis and additive manufacturing science; 2) Materials/structure design enabled by AM and Artificial Intelligence (AI); and 3) Military devices and components enabled by AM and AI. Since 2019, the team has engaged more than 652 undergraduate students in the defense manufacturing education program, supported more than 95 students in funded research and industry projects, and exposed 1300 high school students to advanced defense manufacturing technologies though defense expos , summer camps, and invited talks provided by DoD. The team at UTRGV was recenlty selected by DOE/NNSA and NSF for awards of two large grants ($9 million total) to prepare STEM talents and to advance research at UTRGV, leveraging AM for energy production and critical infrastructures. Currently, the team only has limited access to a Renishaw AM 400 machine located in LA, California, through a collaboration arrangement, which is no longer sufficient to support the research and education programs at UTRGV. The pandemic has additionally caused serious logistic challenges to all operations at every facet. Direct access to modern metal additive manufacturing machines is in desperate need to support a stream of funded projects, support student learning in STEM, and support impactful outreach programs the team offers.

grant.title: Assessment and Planning of Decarbonization Research and Training at UTRGV
grant.abstract: We will conduct an R&D scoping study and university self-assessment to evaluate how the university’s current capabilities, expertise, personnel, facilities and equipment, aligned with FECM objectives. Afterwards, we will identify gaps in capabilities and provide a plan to better prepare UTRGV for potential future competitive solicitations focused on FECM supported technologies. The first objective of this project is to assess existing UTRGV research thrust areas and associated resource capabilities relevant to the mission of FECM to meet the decarbonization goals set for 2035 and 2050. Data on the level of expertise of the relevant faculty/researchers in the focus research areas along with current awards received from all federal agencies on decarbonization research since January 2017 will be collected. Then available faculty expertise, laboratory equipment and other resource capabilities, relevant course offerings and curriculum will be assessed. Afterwards, the focus will be on second objective, which is to assess missing resources to become more competitive in obtaining R&D grants. This objective will involve providing an estimate of the number, relevant experience, and cost of personnel necessary along with how the existing equipment could be modified – and the associated cost – to build the required interdisciplinary team to improve UTRGV’s competitiveness to address future FECM research related opportunities. The overarching objective is to develop student training & education plan to ensure UTRGV’s minority students are prepared to conduct R&D projects. Within this objective, current academic courses, programs, and/or curriculum that aligns with FECM goals will be assessed and then will identify, describe, and develop additional student training. Aligned with this, partner institution, LSU will provide support on student training, including a specialized course on decarbonization, to fill the gaps in our curriculum in a timely manner. The team will also suggest ways in which FECM may support the professional development of minority students from underrepresented and structurally marginalized communities of Rio Grande Valley.

grant.title: Broadening Participation in STEM
grant.other_agencies: The proposal focuses on increasing “effective STEM education and broadening participation” in underrepresented minority STEM students at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) to successfully face academic and professional challenges, recently exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The Freshman Year Innovator Experience proposes the development of self-transformation skills in freshman mechanical engineering students to successfully face academic and professional challenges exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic while working on two parallel projects of technical design innovation and academic career pathways.
grant.abstract: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is located in the historic Texan borderlands created at the end of the Mexican-American war in 1848 which separated families on both sides of the Rio Grande River. The university was formed in 2013 when The University of Texas at Brownsville and The University of Texas Pan-American were consolidated to expand educational opportunities in the underserved and rural Valley of the Rio Grande. UTRGV is a major Hispanic-Serving Institution (HSI), primarily a nonresidential, 4-year, public, R2 institution, with campuses situated along the lower 100 miles of the Rio Grande. UTRGV's student demographics mirror those of the Lower Rio Grande Valley (RGV), with over 95% of our 32,000 students being of Hispanic or Latinx origin (Region One Education Service Center, 2021), and over 85% having Mexican-American heritage. Academic programs in engineering, started in 1992, were first accredited by ABET in 1996. The College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) currently has 6 departments offering 8 bachelors' and 7 masters' degrees. The college has over 110 faculty members and serves nearly 3900 students, mostly (90%) undergraduates. Although CECS does not have a PhD program yet, a pathway for a doctoral degree is offered jointly with the University of Nebraska at Lincoln (UNL). As the second largest HSI in the nation, UTR V is uniquely positioned to broaden the participation of Hispanics in the engineering workforce.

grant.title: Center for Equity in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich (CEE-E3)
Collaborative Effort to Enhance Water Supply for Agriculture and Food Development through Educational Training of Hispanic Professionals
grant.abstract: Currently, there is limited representation of Hispanic in FANH sciences due to limited resources available to recruit and retain them in programs leading to careers in this area. The main purpose of this effort will be to attract and recruit Hispanic students into FANH and related sciences through exemplary outreach activities, K-12 summer experiences, summer internships, and social events. In order to retain the Hispanic students in the FANH sciences disciplines, we will utilize interactive class and lab modules, research-based hands-on experiences, mentoring, student led organization events, professional training sessions, and financial support in the form of research assistantships. The research will focus on water management among various sectors which include food, agriculture, and natural resource development. The research will enable students to interact and learn from professionals in the various sectors of FANH sciences, while also gaining the required knowledge to develop innovative methods that enhance water resource management. These efforts will directly support 64 high school students in summer enrichment camps, 16 undergraduate students through research-based experiences, 6 students through summer internships at USDA agencies, and 2 graduate students with research assistantship. Overall, the program will impact over 8,000 K-12 students through outreach activities and summer camps with over 1,000 undergraduate students in Engineering and Science through designated courses, technical talks, and other professional and social events. We plan to increase the number of students pursuing careers and research positions in FANH sciences through career guidance workshops, internship experiences, and graduate program scholarships. The RGV area is known for its rich agriculture history (sugar cane, citrus orchards and cattle ranching) and economy, and serves as a wonderful setting for promoting FANH sciences among Hispanic.

grant.title: Freshwater Prawn Production: Solving the National Problem of Prawn Postlarvae (Seed) Availability through Engineering and Automation
grant.abstract: The United States imports billions of dollars of shrimp and other seafoods yearly. Farming large freshwater shrimp (i.e., prawns) can help address this deficit. However, although prawns are successfully farmed in Asia and other parts of the world, they have failed to find success in the U.S. The most fundamental problem has been that the hatchery production of seed (i.e., small prawns) is highly technical, labor intensive, and prohibitively expensive to ship, resulting in farmers lacking access to affordable seed. This project proposes to acquire preliminary and proof of concept data for an automated, inexpensive, and simple to use larvae production system that farmers can use to produce prawn seed. The system is called LIKE (Larvae Intensive Kinetic Environment) and uses a downward-thrusting propeller to create water currents that power much of the system’s automation and technical simplicity. Preliminary work by the Applicants has confirmed the basic principles on which the LIKE system operates, however the Applicants lacked the resources to gather the data necessary to demonstrate that the prawn seed problem has been resolved. Seed funding is thus being sought to obtain this necessary data. These data will enable the Applicants to apply for future AFRI grants pertaining to regional hatcheries, adult prawn culture, and the sustainable development of a U.S. prawn industry, all of which have the prerequisite of demonstrating the availability of affordable prawn seed. The broader outcome of this work will be to reduce U.S. dependance on imported shrimp and providing income opportunities to U.S. farmers.

grant.title: Innovative Talented and Achieving Scholars (iTAS) Program: Low Income and Transfer Student Integration and Onboarding Pathways to Increase Student Academic and Career Success in the RGV Engineering & Computer Science Programs
grant.abstract: The ITAS S-STEM program’s mission is to build a foundation in the Rio Grande Valley community and meet the NSF S-STEM goal of supporting and enabling low-income, talented domestic students to pursue successful careers in promising STEM fields. This project will contribute to educate technicians, engineers, and scientists through scholarships and innovative evidence-based curricular and co-curricular activities for all eligible students in the College of Engineering at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). In this proposal, the team at UTRGV, the second largest Hispanic Serving institution in the nation, will also collaborate with South Texas College (STC), the largest community college in the south Texas region with a current S-STEM grant, to increase the success and retention of local transfers students identified to complete their BS degrees.

grant.title: MRI: Acquisition of a nano-scale 3D X-ray microscope for evolutionary, functional, and structural analyses of materials and organisms at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV)
MRI: Acquisition of a single crystal/powder X-ray diffractometer
grant.sponsor_type: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: The objective of this grant application is to acquire a cutting-edge single crystal/powder X-ray diffractometer SC-XRD/PXRD to support fundamental and interdisciplinary research projects and the education program in the South Texas region. The instrument will be installed at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and will support to a broad range of users and will be used as shared instrumentation. The goal of this acquisition is to enable the following: (i) Pursue new research avenues; (ii) Advance current research programs; and (iii) Enhance pedagogical techniques and enrich training in the undergraduate and graduate programs in STEM field. The X-ray diffractometer system will buttress the development of advanced materials at UTRGV in an array of applications, including, but not limited to, electrocatalysis, lithium-ion batteries, molecular catalysis, and ferromagnetic materials. These diverse research thrusts would be substantially aided by state-of-the-art X-ray diffraction with overarching applications in sensors, energy storage, environmental sustainability, protein characterization, organic methodology, and disease diagnosis/treatment. The single crystal X-ray diffractometer allows for the unambiguous determination of the solid-state structure of molecular materials including accurate data on the 3D spatial arrangements of atoms, molecules, the interatomic distance between atoms, bond angles and neighboring atoms. UTRGV is a Hispanic Serving Institution located in South Texas and has the largest Hispanic student population (~90%) in Texas. Individuals from Hispanic ethnicity are historically underrepresented in the STEM workforce and in higher education STEM-disciplines. Faculty members spanning several departments at UTRGV will directly use the requested system for their existing and new research projects as well as the training of highly qualified personnel. Graduate and undergraduate students are expected to take on a leadership role in the proposed interdisciplinary research projects. The acquisition of the X-ray diffractometer will enhance existing outreach efforts with local High school students and teachers during the UTRGV’s summer design camp administered by the research team of this MRI proposal. These integrated activities will unequivocally strengthen research, education, and student participation across programs in chemistry, biology, physics and engineering at UTRGV. In addition, the SC-XRD system will become a tool to bolster regional collaboration of universities and community colleges in South Texas. The personnel exposed to the SC-XRD prioritize fostering an environment of equity and inclusion for underrepresented minority students. Intellectual Merit: The SC-XRD instrument acquisition will enable significant enhancement of basic research toolset across a wide range of materials characterization including but not limited to molecular catalysts, nanomaterials, stimuli-responsive assemblies, supramolecular materials, biological materials, and gas sensors. Determination of molecular structure allows for furthering fundamental understanding of structure-function studies in the interdisciplinary research thrusts in this proposal. Characterization of molecular materials ranging in size from well-defined small molecules to more complex biological systems and solid-state materials is a prerequisite to advance the knowledge of broad research directions at UTRGV. Broader Impacts: The acquisition of the X-ray diffractometer will advance research at UTRGV in the broadly defined areas of materials and biomaterials. The X-ray diffractometer will also enhance the research/educational experience of undergraduate and graduate students at UTRGV from a wide array of science and engineering disciplines. Both the SC-XRD and PXRD will be heavily featured in course curriculum currently offered in the Chemistry, Engineering, and Physics department at UTRGV. The SC-XRD functionality specifically, will foster a research hub in the south-Texas region and bolster collaborative work between researchers at UTRGV and other schools in south Texas including Texas A&M Corpus Christi, Texas A&M Kingsville, and Texas A&M International University. Collaborative efforts between these HSI’s in the south Texas region, will enhance the participation and training of under-represented students in STEM-based disciplines. Continued efforts in outreach to local high schools and community colleges will be enhanced and further recruitment and preparation of local underrepresented populations. The team will ensure that inclusion of women and underrepresented minority students are prioritized in research and educational activities.

Parametric study of a vertical axis wave turbine
grant.sponsor: TEAMER program, supported by Department of Energy
grant.abstract: A wave turbine concept has been proposed in this research. When deployed in waves, the wave induced omnidirectional waterflow drives the turbine rotor into a unidirectional rotation about its vertical axis, which will in turn drive a direct electric generator to produce electricity. The unidirectional rotation of the rotor enables the turbine to respond well in a wide range of wave frequencies with no needs for frequency tuning. The vertical alignment of the rotor makes the turbine tolerant to the wave propagation direction. The proof of concept of this wave turbine has been demonstrated through a preliminary wave flume testing. The TEAMER funding will support numerical modeling and analysis, which are expected to yield an optimized hydrodynamic design of the turbine rotor. The results will be used to guide a scaled prototype development for a comprehensive future testing.

grant.title: Understanding nanofluid reactive transport through porous media.
grant.abstract: Nanoparticles have found extensive applications in various disciplines involving flow of these particles in suspensions through porous media with even reaction involved in several application. However, due to complexity of pore structures, nanoparticle properties, and focus on applications, there is a need for fundamental research to understand and quantify impact of parameters on optimization of nanoparticle applications. This proposed cutting-edge research will study nanoparticle flow in controlled flow geometries using synthetic porous media samples to capture effect of pore structure on fluid flow without competing chemical properties. Additionally, we will account for the effect of chemical properties of porous media and nanoparticles on fluid flow along with impact of reactive flow on nanoparticle flow in controlled synthetic porous media to capture interaction of reaction and nanoparticle transport. Through both experimental and modeling work, this study will be able to produce a more accurate predictive model of reactive nanofluid flow in porous media.

grant.abstract: The Engineering Ambassadors program sponsored by the Halliburton Foundation was designed years ago to recruit top engineering students as summer mentors for Texas Prefreshman Engineering Program (TexPREP). Dr. Stephen Crown (PI) is Professor of Mechanical Engineering and TexPREP Director at UTRGV, which provides 600 top middle/high school students a challenging seven-week academic program that prepares them for careers in STEM. TexPREP goals are to increase the number of students from underrepresented groups (over 40% female, 95% Hispanic and 65% low-income) entering STEM fields; reinforce students’ math preparation; increase college retention; and acquaint students with STEM careers. Ambassadors (engineering and STEM undergrads, expressing interest in oil & gas and 3.0+ GPA) gain valuable leadership experience assisting TexPREP participants with courses and engineering projects throughout the summer program and act as excellent role models for them. Ambassadors participate in a 2-day engineering lab experience with the U.T. Center for Railway Safety directed by Dr. Tarawneh, attend a virtual meeting (via Zoom or Microsoft Teams) with a Halliburton representative to explore employment opportunities, and are encouraged to take a course offered by Dr. Pournik (Petrophysics, drilling and completion, reservoir and production, and natural gas engineering). These opportunities will shape their career paths and give the Ambassadors a rich experience to share with TexPREP students.

Specifically, this proposal seeks to pilot 1) a clam hatchery in Texas using the native clam (M. campechiensis), 2) the suitability of grow-out at a site in the Lower Laguna Madre (LLM, Fig. 1-2), and 3) integrating educational tours and displays on sustainable bivalve farming to the existing educational offerings at UTRGV’s Coastal Studies Lab located on the LLM (Fig. 1-1).

grant.title: Community, Innovation, and Resilience Program
grant.abstract: The “Community, Innovation, & Resilience” program will foster intercultural dialogue among the participants as they identify issues or problems in the Rio Grande Valley region of South Texas and work together to provide potential solutions using science and engineering concepts, which is a priority topic. The participants from Iran, Iraq, and Oman will learn about this region and work with the UTRGV participants to tackle real problems. In this process, the usual narrative is flipped, as students from the Middle East will provide assistance to local technical problems in the USA. This program will use free, mobile communication software such as WhatsApp. Facilitators will guide participant teams through a series of dialogues designed to identify a problem, research possible solutions, and present a proposal. The purpose of this program is to provide participants with an educational experience that both fosters intercultural understanding and real-world design engineering. The program will embed the Virtual Exchange university courses in STEM disciplines. The deliverables for the Virtual Exchange projects will be limited in scope and will be paced over several weeks to allow students to communicate and interact with one another at each stage. UTRGV launched a VE program in the summer of 2020 with an initial cohort of three professors paired with three professors from foreign partner institutions. Three more pairs are receiving training now for Spring 2021. This program was funded by the Undergraduate International Studies and Foreign Languages Program of the US Dept of Ed, which is ending in November 2020. We hope to expand and continue this program through the Stevens Initiative grant. A priority for this project is to train and establish virtual exchange facilitators that offer recurring university courses. Faculty learning groups will allow facilitators to support each other after the grant ends.
