grant.title: CREST Center for Multidisciplinary Research Excellence in Cyber-Physical Infrastructure Systems (MECIS)
grant.abstract: Overview: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) proposes to establish the “CREST Center for Multidisciplinary Research Excellence in Cyber-Physical Infrastructure Systems (MECIS).” The Center’s mission is to advance and transform the much-needed research and education at the nexus of automation, sensors, and artificial intelligence (AI), as integral parts of the “NSF’s 10 Big Ideas,” anticipating the revolutionary cyber-physical infrastructure systems (CIS). Three Colleges of Engineering, Sciences, and Education at UTRGV in collaboration with the Universities of Illinois (at Urbana-Champaign and at Chicago) and California (Riverside) will pursue multidisciplinary research on CIS, aiming to: (i) transfer technology to various transportation, logistics, manufacturing, and construction industries; and (ii) prepare a minority STEM workforce to drive future CIS-based communities. The Center envisions a portfolio of three research subprojects on automation, sensors, and AI that bridges diverse STEM disciplines. A holistic, multi-level approach is adopted to address CIS planning, design, and operation. While each subproject constitutes a unique element, their synergy ensures the CIS integrity. Subproject 1 pushes the frontiers of knowledge in future transportation infrastructure, which will be transformed by autonomous vehicles (AVs) and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), in six directions: (i) at the planning level, public acceptance and policy issues of (U)AV; (ii-iv) at the design level, computer vision, automatic navigation, and model/field-based testing of the designed capabilities; and (v, vi) at the operation level, human-(U)AV interactions and network-wide inter-(U)AV interactions. Subproject 2 designs and embeds sensors in CIS for two purposes. First, (U)AV sensors help perform automated tasks. Second, sensors in civil infrastructure and (U)AVs monitor infrastructure health. Three research areas are defined: (i, ii) at the design level, computational simulation, synthesis, and 3D printing of sensor materials and UAV structures, and (iii) at the operation level, cost-effective decision-making to upkeep infrastructure health using sensor data. Since (U)AVs and sensors will inherently generate big data, Subproject 3 will synchronously work with subprojects 1 and 2 to: (i) develop AI solutions for big data management, and (ii) develop AI algorithms for big data analytics and decision making in the design and operation of (U)AVs and infrastructure. UTRGV is the nation’s second largest Hispanic-Serving Institute (HIS) located in South Texas with an established record of preparing underrepresented minority students for STEM careers. The Center will provide (under)graduate students with cutting-edge CIS research experience, will integrate CIS research and education, and will pave a pathway from High School through graduate programs in STEM disciplines. This broad initiative at UTRGV will also offer new courses related to the subprojects. The Center will further enhance the research infrastructure at UTRGV and will strengthen the research competitiveness of a diverse group of faculty. Intellectual Merit: The proposed self-sustaining Center will play a key role in transforming the scientific discoveries at the intersection of automation, sensors, and AI technologies, which are the integral elements of next-generation CIS. The Center will address current gaps in the planning, design, and operation of CIS by proposing innovative theoretical, computational, experimental, and empirical solutions spanning from micro (molecule)- to macro (system)-scale, which also yield practical solutions valuable for the industry. Broader Impacts: The Center’s research and education activities will develop an underrepresented workforce equipped with the skills to address complex societal problems. The Center will partner with the public and private sectors to advance technology transfer and product development in CIS. The Center’s activities are key for the establishment of an inaugural engineering doctoral program, which will be vital in elevating UTRGV to a Research I institution and advancing the CIS research agenda in a predominantly HSI. The Center's research findings will be made available to the research community as journal publications and conference proceedings, which will inform other domains undergoing related transformations, such as the health industry, manufacturing and production systems, and the military.

grant.title: Development of a vertical-axis unidirectional wave turbine for low-cost electricity
grant.abstract: A point-absorber-type wave energy converter (WEC)—a vertical axis unidirectional wave turbine—is proposed. The turbine has a submerged rotor with a hydrodynamically optimized blade shape and layout, an elongated vertical shaft reaching out of water, and a gearbox-coupled electric generator with data-driven power control connected to the distal end of the shaft. The turbine is supported by a floating platform, which is secured at the testing site through slack mooring. The uniqueness and innovation are reflected in the turbine’s operating principle: The turbine’s rotor performs unidirectional rotation about a vertical axis in omnidirectional water flows in waves. The unidirectional rotation makes the turbine wave-frequency tolerant. The vertical axis orientation makes the turbine wave-direction tolerant. Both features enable the turbine a very simple and robust structure with a low cost and long service time. This operating principle will augment the WEC family with a novel WEC type that contrasts with reciprocating WECs and horizontal-axis cyclic WECs. The turbine concept has been validated through extensive wave flume testing. Potential risks in PacWave testing may include water leak into the generator and accidental blade damage. Conservative and modular designs for long endurance and easy replacement will be pursued in collaboration with industrial partners. Two research centers from UTRGV and MSU will provide support with state-of-the-art fabrication facilities.

grant.title: Development of fluid flow equation for flow through porous medium and fracture network using synthetic media
grant.sponsor: American Chemical Society Petroleum Research Fund
grant.abstract: While there has been extensive research on understanding fluid flow in porous media, the majority of these have used complex porous media samples from outcrops or actual reservoirs, resulting in failure to account accurately for the fundamental impact of various pore parameters on fluid flow. There have been studies on the impact of fractures on fluid flow but have faced similar issues due to lack of control on fracture patterns and structural parameters. Hence, our study aims to create a controlled porous structure with the inclusion of fractures in order to determine the underlying mechanism controlling fluid flow in such porous structure networks, which will capture the impact of various porous structure parameters on fluid flow. As a result of this study, a comprehensive model will be developed that will accurately predict fluid flow in porous media and fracture networks. This will enable more accurate oil and gas production rate estimation from various pore structure reservoirs in addition to reservoirs with natural or induced fractures. Furthermore, this research will promote further research on strategies to generate porous structures, including fractures that maximize productivity from reservoirs.

grant.title: DoD-HBCUMI Equipment: Acquisition of an Advanced Materials’ Surface Characterization System for Science and Engineering Research and Education at South Texas
grant.abstract: The objective of this proposal is to acquire a state of the art surface characterization system including nano-indentation, micro-indentation, micro-scratch tester, and AFM that will support multidisciplinary research projects and education programs in areas of interest to DoD at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). The proposed system will include cutting-edge features needed to characterize a broad range of materials and provide the capability to investigate mechanical, tribological and other physical properties at nanostructured scales for materials that are too thin to be tested using conventional methods. In addition, UTRGV has in place a magnetron sputtering system (AJA International, A300) for research in physical vapor deposition (PVD). The acquisition of the proposed equipment will allow the surface characterization of the materials created by the sputtering system, which will immediately benefit research and educational projects in areas of interest to DoD. These projects include the following: (1) High temperature characterization of novel thermal barrier coatings created by PVD. Encompassing the development of novel PVD protective thermal barrier coatings TBC for gas turbine engines and the analytical methods to study their mechanical properties and adhesion to turbine blade materials at elevated temperatures. (2) Cost-effective CIGS thin films for novel solar power technology, encompassing the development of thin film solar cell like Copper Indium Gallium Di-Selenide (CIGS) with an optimized design considering the efficiency and cost effectiveness, to be used for space and satellite applications. Further, theoretical and numerical models will be developed, and the simulated result will be compared with experimental data. (3) Investigation of additive synthesis of intermetallic (IM) containing high entropy alloys (HEAs) directly from pure elemental powders using multiple metal additive manufacturing processes. Research in HEAs will open a nearly infinite space for novel engineering materials with trans-scale structures delivering superior properties required in extreme conditions normally expected in many defense systems. (4) Biointerfacing of functional nanofilaments for health/biothreat monitoring and life research. This project aims for the development of a novel functional system: Biohazard and Radiation Sensing (BRS). Integrated functional materials (IFM) will be grafted onto functional metal oxide with an immediate successive mesoporous micro layer surrounded by composite oxides. Advanced integrated materials systems with an innovative embedded BRS sensor system for real-time monitoring of biological and radiation hazards will be developed. (5) High energy density nanostructured composites with tailored particles size and shapes. The development of novel nanoenergetic materials, their design, synthesis and fabrication procedures are critical for national security and it was recognized as a significant addition to support advanced military formulations. The goal of this project is to explore the physics-based knowledge in energy release, shock waves and pressure discharge needed to enhance the performance and functionality of novel high density nanoenergetic composites with tailored particle shapes and size to reduce the mass and volume of munitions systems and components. The instrument will form a nucleus for a broad collaboration of scholars, resulting in further funding opportunities. Additionally, the proposed equipment will facilitate efforts at UTRGV to reach out to traditionally underrepresented groups within science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields. The opportunity to participate in a state-of-the-art research projects motivates UTRGV students from a diverse background to pursue graduate school (M.S. or Ph.D. degrees). Furthermore, the acquisition of the proposed equipment will support development of physics, materials science, and engineering doctoral programs. Lastly, the proposed equipment will support the educational programs developed by the consortium for Innovation Driven Research/Education Ecosystem for Advanced Manufacturing for the Defense (I-DREAM4D) directed by Dr. J. Li at UTRGV.

grant.title: ERI: Fundamental understanding of vegetable oil-based nanolubricants for industrial applications
grant.abstract: Project Summary Overview: The objective of this research project is to acquire fundamental understanding of the effects of different types of nanoparticles, surfactants, and concentrations on the rheological behavior, thermophysical properties, and tribological performance of vegetable oil-based nanolubricants. According to new studies, about 23% of the world ́s energy consumption is spent to overcome friction between moving components and to replace or repair worn tooling and materials. In the context of energy efficiency, the significance of reducing friction cannot be overemphasized. This is especially true as oil reserves continue to decrease and energy costs are rising relentlessly. Most current lubricants contain petroleum base stocks, which are toxic to the environment and difficult to dispose of. Recently, due to environmental issues and increased regulations over contamination and pollution, there has been a growing concern on the use of mineral oils as lubricants. This concern has promoted a need for renewable and biodegradable lubricants. Currently, vegetable oils are being investigated as a potential source of environmentally favorable lubricants, due to a combination of biodegradability, renewability and excellent lubrication performance. Vegetable oils have enormous potential as alternatives and replacements for mineral oil in a myriad of industrial applications. However, one of the main disadvantages is their poor performance when working at high temperature and pressure. In the recent decade, there has been attention for the use of nanoparticles in many types of base fluids. Nanoparticles have attracted considerable interest in recent years because of their excellent physical and chemical properties. However, inorganic nanoparticles very easily agglomerate in many mediums and have poor dispersive capacity in organic solvents and oil. Intellectual Merit: This project will be the first comprehensive study focused on the effect of nanoparticles with different characteristics (morphology, size) at different concentrations on the rheological behavior, thermophysical properties, and the tribological performance of vegetable oil-based nanolubricants. One of the main challenges will be to formulate stable suspensions because sediments and agglomerates will form over long period of the nanolubricants in stationary condition. Therefore, different surfactants and treatments will be used for the nanolubricants preparation. The fundamental understanding obtained will help to investigate the relation between the rheological behavior and thermophysical properties, on the tribological performance of the vegetable oil-based nanolubricants, and real applications. In addition, a model will be crated to predict the behavior based on nanoparticle characteristics, surfactant, concentrations, and type of vegetable oil. Broader Impacts: The broader impacts the proposed project may have are several and will significantly impact UTRGV transition towards an emerging research institution. If successful, this study will facilitate the fundamental understanding of characteristics that enable us to design and develop vegetable oil-based nanolubricants with superior tribological performance. Also, it will help to revitalize American manufacturing, to grow the national prosperity and workforce, and to reshape strategic industries. Most of the activities planned will be carried out by undergraduate and M.S. students. Specifically, the proposed project will strengthen existing courses as a result of this funding. In addition, one of the primary goals of The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is to provide the opportunity of being engaged in high level research to as many undergraduate and graduate students as possible, as they pursue their degrees. With the training planned by the PI, undergraduate and graduate students will be capable of assisting in the development of new and novel products and the experimentation required for their characterization. The ability to contribute in a meaningful way to this level of science and engineering not only engages the student in the research but also has a direct and extremely positive impact on their retention, performance in their coursework, and their desire and ability to pursue graduate level education.

Furthermore, in order to promote engineering, especially interest in the oil and gas sector, during the spring semester, when middle and high school students (around 200) from various school districts visit the campus, the lab will be open and experiments will be demonstrated to them. In the summer, when several K-12 camps occur on campus (around 200), especially in the engineering college, we will hold sessions to showcase the experiments to the campers to promote greater interest in pursuing study in disciplines that relate to the oil and gas industry.

IntelligentSelf-Powered Wireless Sensing (ISPWS) System for Onboard Real-time Health Monitoring and Proactive Damage Detection of Freight Trains
grant.sponsor: The National Academies of Sciences Engineering Medicine
grant.abstract: Ensuring the safety of the freight railway network is essential for enabling the safe, reliable, and efficient movement of goods in the United States. Freight railcars are susceptible to wheel misalignment due to excessive speeding on curves, track defects, and failures of the critical components of their suspension systems that is usually caused by hunting oscillation, overheating, and impact. The current practice for condition monitoring of the critical components of freight railcars, such as wheel bearings, relies on trackside methods which are based on the deployment of sensors on the track in isolated locations. These methods are inherently “reactive,” implying that they resort to an unappealing find-and-fix strategy which act only when the target component is already damaged. In addition, they require a large amount of external power which makes them costly. The objective of this research proposal is to develop the proof-of-concept prototype of an onboard self-powered wireless sensing system for real-time health monitoring and prediction of the wheel bearings of freight railcars by employing a “proactive” damage detection strategy developed based on online machine learning . The wireless sensing system is battery-less and is powered by an onboard electromagnetic energy harvester with a high-power density.

grant.title: Large-scale CoPe: CIRCLE: AI and Modeling for Collective Impact on Resilient Communities through Social Learning and Equity
grant.other_agencies: The CIRCLE-inG project is a place-based university-community collaboration to describe and find solutions for local coastal issues, linking with co-design approaches and cutting-edge convergence models for compound and cascading hazards with a special focus on flooding.
grant.abstract: As part of the CIRCLE project, UTRGV will participate in strong support of the proposed convergent research that looks at how data from sensors can inform the creation of flood and disaster model and how that data can be used to support stakeholder dialogue and engagement/co-design. As part of this research team, UTRGV scientists will leverage existing research efforts on soil moisture across agronomic landscape to evaluate how soil infiltration rates influence (1) water levels during flooding, (2) soil moisture which impacts crop yields. We will provide this data to the CIRCLE team who will help couple and refine hydraulic models with crop models that (3) help us better understand conservation tradeoffs / problem formulation / and potential intervention options for farmers and rural residents in the south Texas region.

grant.title: LEAPS-MPS: Exploring Centrifugal Jet Spinning of Ultra-High-Temperature Ceramic Nanofibers
grant.sponsor_type: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: This research project consists of a novel method to fabricate micro- and nano-sized ceramic fibers that can withstand several thousand degrees Celsius without melting. A metal salt and a polymer are dissolved to make a viscous solution that is subsequently spun into fibers. The fibers are then heat treated to react the metal with the carbon in the polymer and form the ultra-high-temperature ceramic fiber. The effects of high temperatures and oxygen in the atmosphere on the fibers’ microstructure are also studied. This research makes it possible to fabricate, in large quantities and at low temperature, ceramic nanofiber mats of compounds not available in fiber form. These ultra-high temperature ceramic fiber mats can contribute to thermal protection systems that allow aircraft, missiles, and rockets to travel faster and for a longer period at hypersonic speed. Two undergraduate students and two graduate students from a minority-serving institution are obtaining laboratory experience in ceramic manufacturing and testing. Another 8 – 16 undergraduate students are engaged in designing, fabricating, and testing equipment for ceramic materials characterization. These graduates typically find employment in the high-tech industry or further pursue graduate degrees.

grant.title: MRI: Acquisition of a Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) for Advanced Materials Research and Education Programs at the Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: PROJECT SUMMARY Overview: The objective of the present MRI proposal is to acquire a state-of-the-art Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) that will support interdisciplinary research and education programs at UTRGV. The STEM combines the principles of transmission electron microscopy and scanning electron microscopy. The proposed instrument (TalosTM F200i) is flexible and compact 200 kV Field Emission Gun (FEG) STEM, designed for precise and quantitative characterization of nanomaterials and biological cells. It combines an outstanding quality in high-resolution STEM imaging with Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS). In addition, the instrument is equipped with tomographic capabilities via software for alignment of a tomographic series of images, and 3D reconstruction of the data. Intellectual Merit: The acquisition of the TalosTM F200i STEM instrument will enable a significant enhancement of basic research toolset across a wide range of materials, medical education and research programs including Chemistry, Physics, Medicine and Mechanical, Electrical and Manufacturing Engineering at UTRGV. Specifically, the proposed equipment will support projects to advance the development and characterization of different nanoparticles as lubricant additives, composite nanofibers, high entropy alloys (HEA) prepared by Selective Laser Melting technology, regenerative medicine, polymers, and nanomaterials for use in , patterned magnetic arrays, temperature controlled drug delivery systems, bioimaging, nanostructured energetic devices, semiconductors, high temperature superconductors, and radiation induced functional materials. The acquisition of the STEM will broaden the research scope for all participants, making it possible to address new scientific challenges in new transformative research directions. Broader Impacts: This proposal brings together a diverse group of faculty members and will significantly impact UTRGV transition towards an emerging research institution. In addition, most of the projects will be carried out by undergraduate and M.S. students. Specifically, the instrument will strengthen existing courses and several more will be developed as a result of this funding. Additionally, it will significantly support research and education programs operated at the DoD I-DREAM4D Consortium, which was recently funded by DoD on a $4 million grant and NSF PREM funded projects. It can also be integrated in the K12 outreach and education efforts organized by the colleges and the consortium at national scale. Results from the research projects supported by this instrument will be disseminated in peer journal articles and national/international conferences to stimulate further understanding and progress of the various research areas of the investigators discussed in this proposal. More importantly, this proposal will:1) Promote a hands-on, entrepreneurial, educational experience, and training of graduate and undergraduate students in advanced materials, nanomaterial design, biomaterials and characterization; 2) Enhance the research infrastructure at UTRGV; 3) Enhance the interdisciplinary research partnership between different departments at UTRGV to better compete for external funding; and 4) Increase the Hispanic Student retention rate at UTRGV In summary, the TalosTM F200i instrument acquisition will strengthen the existing materials and medical research infrastructure at UTRGV and enhance the research and educational experiences of many students at UTRGV and South Texas region.

grant.title: NSF FM SG Cyber
grant.abstract: Overview: Rapid changes in technology, customer preferences, and customer choices are making a significant impact on Future Manufacturing. These fast changes are making seismic shifts in the workforce environment too. It is imperative to train our future students and workers for this dynamic shift in the manufacturing environment. It is possible only if we develop a clear understanding of the changing ecosystem of Future Manufacturing. We are witnessing many technological, demographic, and consumption changes. Industry 4.0 has destined that Future Manufacturing will be Distributed Manufacturing. COVID-19 has shown the magnitude of disruption for the Vertically Integrated Centralized Manufacturing (VICM), perpetuated by the Chinese Establishment. Even if this Chinese model has given the consumers a significant cost advantage, the present pandemic has suddenly made the fault line of this model obvious and glaring in terms of uncertainty in product delivery, quality, and even product substitution. Given this unprecedented disruption, we are proposing an alternative model of Globally Balanced Distributed Manufacturing (GBDM). The proposed model will take full advantage of Industry 4.0 and offer customers guaranteed delivery on time and Quality. Intellectual Merit: We are proposing a Globally Balanced Distributed Manufacturing (GBDM) system that is digitally connected using AI-augmented Cloud service. Our model will identify customer needs using a novel platform called Edited Platform proposed by one of our Co-PIs. A digital avatar of the proposed product will be transmitted via secured Blockchain to a local manufacturer who will convert the digital art into a physical part. This will not only guarantee both Quality and deliverability, but the enterprise manufacturer can also add a local touch (product to packaging) to the product for the customer. Our model is based on AI (Artificial Intelligence) augmented Secured Cloud-Based Smart Additive Manufacturing. During COVID 19 lockdown our graduating mechanical engineering students completed their product designs at home and the teammates independently checked the design in different physical locations. Finally, our Graduate Research Assistants printed the design for demonstration in yet another physical location. This process validated the concept of Distributed Manufacturing. The customer, design engineer, manufacturer, and the business enterprise can be in several different geographical locations, yet they can communicate and manufacture the product. We are proposing to generalize this concept of AI-augmented Cloud-based Smart Additive Manufacturing for any design, simple or complex. The expertise of our Co-PIs includes Edited Platform, Network Security, and Distributed Manufacturing, among others. We plan to add a few selected AI features to improve the Quality of 3D Printed parts. We have an excellent collaborative relationship with local manufacturers to validate this model as noted by the Support Letters. Broader Impacts: To prepare our workforce for Future Manufacturing, universities have a big role to play. We need to prepare our students in relevant areas like computer skills, robotics, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Blockchain technology, network security, and Smart Manufacturing. They need to also understand the basic concepts of Globally Balanced Distributed Manufacturing, Network Security, and, of course, Smart Additive Manufacturing (SAM). We are a Minority-Serving Hispanic University with more than 30,000 students who are bi-lingual and bi-cultural. Our students are poised to take advantage of Future Manufacturing aka Industry 4.0. Local industries are excited to take advantage of this opportunity by collaborating with the University and offering our students needed training and opportunities. This Fund will both validate the concept and train our students for many jobs that do not exist today. The University has an established training center for our students and local community called TMAC (Texas Manufacturing Assistance Center). This funding can fully leverage that program with a relatively modest investment.

grant.title: UTRGV-UMN PARTNERSHIP to Strengthen the PREM Pathway
grant.abstract: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) located in the southernmost region of Texas serves over 31,000 students, of whom 89% are Hispanic. UTRGV is 2nd in the nation in total Hispanic enrollment and 3rd in graduating Hispanics. The proposed Partnership for Research and Education in Materials (PREM) between UTRGV and the University of Minnesota (UMN) Materials Research Science and Engineering Center (MRSEC) will focus particularly on retention and degree attainment of underrepresented minority undergraduates, as well as on building the graduate school pipeline where Hispanic students are even more underrepresented. The PREM pathway goals are to achieve a 5-year graduation rate of at least 85% for PREM undergraduate students and a graduate school enrollment rate of at least 30% for PREM alumni. This PREM aims to provide intensive research opportunities to at least 100 undergraduate students during the course of the award. Students will develop expertise in the broad areas of energy and smart materials while acquiring a strong set of multi-disciplinary skills in fundamental research. The participating students will carry out research at both academic institutions and will be mentored by faculty from several disciplines. Mentoring of junior and mid-career faculty will also be fostered. This PREM program will allow UTRGV to significantly accelerate its emergence as a focal center for materials research and develop a long-lasting collaborative partnership with UMN. The research results under the UTRGV-UMN PREM partnership will be disseminated in peer-reviewed journals and conferences, and to the public at large via a dedicated web portal and frequent presentations at local K-12 schools. The UTRGV-UMN PREM will engage in compelling scientific materials research through a synergistic approach towards development of next-generation nanofiber (NF) systems that could impact a large number of important practical applications, including in the biomedical fields, filtration, electronics and energy related sectors. The team proposes to develop a suite of strategies to prescribe, tailor, design and control the mesostructures of fine fibers. UTRGV’s world leadership in force-spinning leverages its platform in NF process-structure-characterization, while design and characterization of nanoscale structures match a distinguishing strength of the UMN MRSEC. The team will produce tunable hierarchical structures with powerful property combinations. The proposed research is organized around two interdisciplinary research groups (IRG); the first will explore processing routes to control both fiber geometry and internal structure, and the second will adapt internally structured NFs for specific applications. The world-class instrument facilities at UMN will enable and catalyze the research efforts and will provide unique opportunities for cross-fertilization of ideas, mentoring, and multidisciplinary training. The collaborative teams will hold research-focus group meetings via real-time video teleconferencing and hold an annual symposium hosted by each institution, rotating yearly. This will foster a high-level of research activity and a well-orchestrated student-centered organizational environment. Ultimately, this research partnership will increase understanding of hierarchically designed NFs and will pave the way for novel systems with potential to facilitate decentralized energy production in the world.

Cost and energy savings in industrial activities across the US-Mexico border through environmentally friendly vegetable-oil based nano-lubricants
grant.abstract: The present innovative collaborative research project comprises a joint effort between The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and Universidad de Monterrey (UDEM) to develop and evaluate new environmentally friendly vegetable-oil based nano-lubricants to support industrial activities across the US-Mexico border and promote energy savings specifically in the metal-mechanic industry. According to new studies, about 23% of the world ́s energy consumption is spent to overcome friction between moving components and to replace or repair worn tooling and materials. In the context of energy efficiency, the significance of reducing friction cannot be overemphasized. This is especially true as oil reserves continue to decrease and energy costs are rising relentlessly. Most current lubricants contain petroleum base stocks, which are toxic to environment and difficult to dispose of after use. Recently, due to environmental issues and growing regulations over contamination and pollution there has been a growing concern on the use of mineral oils as lubricants. This concern has promoted a need for renewable and biodegradable lubricants. Since we live on a planet with finite resources, we must think about the future generations and work for a sustainable development in the field of tribology. Currently, vegetable oils are being investigated as a potential source of environmentally favorable lubricants, due to a combination of biodegradability, renewability and excellent lubrication performance. Based on common research interests, the main aim of the present collaborative research project is to develop new vegetable-oil based nano-lubricants by combining vegetable oils available in Texas and Mexico and environmentally friendly nanoclays. If awarded, the ConTEX collaborative research project will promote a strong collaboration between faculty and students form UTRGV and UDEM and will act as a vehicle to expose more engineering students to scientific research, to provide them with more opportunities to publish in scientific journals and present their work at symposiums, as well as to better prepare them to enter the STEM workforce and/or encourage them to pursue advanced degrees.

Energy transfer between waves and a unidirectional rotor in wave energy conversion
grant.abstract: The main objective of the proposed work is to gain a fundamental understanding of the energy transfer process between ocean waves and a novel class of wave energy converters (WECs), originated and validated by the PI. The novelty and potentially transformative nature of this project derives from the joint effort of three approaches to reveal flow physics in wave-WEC interaction from the energy transfer perspective: experimental study, computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and phenomenological modeling. This proposed research into harvesting ocean wave energy will advance the knowledge base on designing and optimizing WECs. Presently, there is a global effort to strive for alternative, renewable, energy sources. The oceans are a huge reservoir, largely untapped, of constantly renewing energy carried by ocean waves, known as "Blue Energy.” Tapping into Blue Energy presents its own unique challenges. The constantly changing nature of water flow in waves requires that efficient energy conversion occurs for all possible flow directions in a dynamic fashion. The research findings of this work will lay the foundation for WEC development and provide an experimentally-verified theoretical framework that will enable the creation of efficient WEC devices that maximize wave-to-WEC energy transfer and minimize the reverse. These novel WECs of the PI’s design have a rotor performing unidirectional rotation about a vertical axis in waves; that is in contrast to the reciprocating motion of most other WEC technologies. A basic rotor, consisting of both horizontal and vertical hydrofoil blades, is to be employed. The wave-rotor interaction will be studied experimentally using a laboratory wave flume, and theoretically using both detailed CFD modeling and intuitive phenomenological modeling techniques. All three approaches will be compared and will augment one another to obtain a full understanding of the wave-rotor energy transfer mechanism. Upon success, this project will make a huge impact in our ability to harvest Blue Energy. Using this proposed research as a platform, a new, collaborative model of engineering education will be demonstrated between two neighboring institutions on either side of the U.S.-Mexico border.

This project provides innovative ways for adapting effective evidence based curricular and co-curricular activities aimed to improve undergraduate student academic success. The primary goal of this project is to encourage and increase the number of students towards obtaining their degrees in STEM by providing 30 undergradaute students with four-year scholarships, and 17 undergraduate students with two-year scholarships (47 total), spread across four cohorts. In addition, we emphasize on improved student technical workforce readiness levels by establishing an academic support system at the College of Engineering and Computer Science (COECS) to encourage students to pursue careers in emerging fields of engineering and technology. Building on existing student support services at UTRGV, this project includes technical and academic success workshops, professional development, peer mentoring, industry certifications and internships, and developing course modules integrated with Engineering Technology and Manufacturing Engineering curriculum. The objectives identified to meet the primary project goal include: (a) To increase student enrollment of Manufacturing and Engineering Technology undergraduate programs created to train and prepare students with high-tech skills in the fields of manufacturing, automation and systems engineering; (b) Developing an Eco-System in COECS with tailored student centric activities to address student’s precollege experience, social-cultural experience, institutional experience, and college experience specifically targeting underrepresented demographics; (c) Financially support undergraduate students by awarding S-STEM scholarships over the grant period; and (d) Build partnerships with industry to provide more learning and internship opportunities for students.

grant.title: Ocean-based and nature-powered humidification-dehumidification desalination
grant.abstract: A novel process to desalinate seawater is to be developed through the proposed work. Specifically, an ocean-based and nature-powered humidification-dehumidification (HDH) desalination process will be demonstrated in a lab scale. Innovative approaches include: (i) a floating system directly situated in the coastal water with no seawater intake and no brine discharge, (ii) a fully nature-powered mechanism directly driven by multiple renewable energy sources with zero usage of electricity, and (iii) a unique humidifier design using cloth wetting and wave overtopping to enhance mass transfer. The enabled desalination plant will be simple, robust, and environmentally-friendly, and is expected to produce freshwater in both large and small scales cost-effectively to meet diverse needs. Water quality analysis will be conducted in parallel with the technological advancement. The requested funds will be used to cover expenses on: wages for three graduate research assistants, summer salaries for three faculty members (the applicants), materials and supplies for the lab-scale prototype construction and water quality analysis, small instruments for testing the prototype, travel fees, and indirect costs. The proposed project will contribute to accomplishing the objectives 1, 2, 4, 5 defined in Water Desalination Act of 1996 as amended by WIIN Act and the objective 5 defined in Desalination 2008 , as listed in page 2 of the FOA.

grant.title: Ultra-High Temperature Transition Metal Carbide Nanofibers Developed by Centrifugal Jet Spinning
grant.abstract: Hypersonic vehicles travel many times faster than the speed of sound. Such great speed can cause the surfaces of an aircraft to heat up to very high temperatures. The need exists[AL1] to develop materials that can withstand the extreme heat. The research project will consist of testing a novel method to fabricate micro- and nano-sized ceramic fibers used to insulate and protect hypersonic aircraft during flights. A metal salt and a polymer will be dissolved to make a viscous solution that will then be spun into fiber form. The fibers will be heated so that the metal reacts with the carbon in the polymer, without destroying the fibers, to make carbide fiber mats that can withstand several thousand degrees without melting. The effects of high temperatures and oxygen in the atmosphere on the fibers’ microstructure will also be studied. If successful, these ultra-high temperature ceramic fiber mats can contribute to thermal protection systems that will allow aircraft, missiles, and rockets to travel faster, and for a longer period, at hypersonic speed.

grant.title: Understanding the structure-processing-properties relationship of novel hyper organic/inorganic materials for catalytic applications
grant.abstract: Alumina (Al2O3) is widely used as catalyst support media in the Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) processes of crude oil due to its textural properties such as surface area and their acid/base characteristics. However, the chemical and hydrothermal stability of Al2O3 are still a critical point for catalytic applications due to many challenges, which may block the active sites of the catalyst resulting in catalyst instability. Strategies for minimizing these problems have involved the use of carbon, TiO2, silica and carbon nanotubes as alternative catalyst supports due to their high surface area, strong metal support interaction, and acid-base properties. This proposal involves the use of Forcespinning (FS) of a high melting point polymer to fabricate polymer/ceramic composite fibers as a catalyst support in heterogeneous catalysis. The current proposal focuses on establishing a fundamental understanding of the relationships between processing, structure, composition, and performance of polymer fibers to improve the manufacturability of the material and to understand how the interaction between the polymer fibers and catalyst nanoparticles. Successful demonstration of the proposed work will lead to new understanding of the fundamental questions: Can polymer-supported catalysts extend the catalysis operational range beyond its current capabilities? and Can polymer-supported catalysts provide a significant advancement in understanding the behavior of catalyst support materials under operating conditions? Our hypothesis is that unlike traditionally extruded oxide supported catalysts, polymer forcespun-supported catalysts should have lighter weights, higher activity, better packing densities resulting in longer life times for the catalysts.

Laser surface texturing technology to decrease the energy consumption and improve the performance of transportation infrastructure roller bearings
grant.abstract: The objective of the present research project is to investigate the use of a new technology of laser surface texturing to improve the performance, durability, and decrease the energy consumption of transportation infrastructure bearings. The growing emphasis on cost-effectiveness and energy-efficiency has significantly resulted in elevating adoption of bearings across varied application areas. These applications include roadways (e.g. agriculture, industrial, automotive, mining, and construction), railways and ports. The proposed study will include the surface modification of cylindrical-roller bearing components through laser surface texturing (LST) technology and the experimental and numerical acquisition of bearing operational data as a function of load, speed, time, ambient temperature, and bearing condition. The bearing operational data to be collected include operational temperature, vibration signals, and energy consumption (current). Also, the tribological behavior, including coefficient of friction (COF) and wear, of different LST patterns will be evaluated trough tribological tests using block-on-ring configuration. Collaborators have already developed a thermal finite element model that can simulate some normal and abnormal bearing operating conditions. Using experimental results, the PI’s will study the correlation between tribological behavior and operating conditions of different LST patterns on cylindrical-roller bearings. The developed correlation can then be used to determine the impact of laser surface texturing to maximize the bearing durability. It will also provide the opportunity to use the enhanced operating conditions while the texturizing lasts to estimate the life remaining in the bearing components. In addition, the developed correlation provides insight into possible areas of improvement for the next generation of transportation infrastructure bearings with improved performance and extended life.

grant.abstract: The objective of this Major Research Instrumentation (MRI) proposal is to acquire a cutting-edge mechanical surface characterization platform including nanoindentation, micro-indentation, micro-scratch tester, and AFM that will support multidisciplinary research and education programs at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). Nanoindentation is used to probe the mechanical properties of materials at the nano-size scale (approximately 10 -7 to 10 -9 meters). The system will include features needed to characterize a broad range of materials such as nanocrystalline alloys, polymer nanocomposite films, thin hard films, semiconductors, and conducting films from metallic nanoparticle dispersion precursors. The mechanical surface characterization platform will provide critical information about the behavior of materials for a variety of scientific and engineering challenges. It will create new opportunities to integrate research, education, training, and outreach. The capability to probe mechanical properties at nano-size scales is required for films that are too thin to test using conventional methods and for other materials whose properties are engineered by manipulating their structure at these small length scales. In addition, UTRGV has in place a magnetron sputtering system (AJA International, A300) for research in physical vapor deposition (PVD). The system is capable to create thin PVD ceramic films for different research areas. The acquisition of the mechanical surface characterization platform will immediately benefit research and educational projects in engineering, materials science, chemistry and physics at UTRGV.

grant.title: Ocean-based and nature-powered humidification-dehumidification desalination
grant.abstract: A novel process to desalinate seawater is to be developed through the proposed work. Specifically, an ocean-based and nature-powered humidification-dehumidification (HDH) desalination process will be demonstrated in a lab scale. Innovative approaches include: (i) a floating system directly situated in the coastal water with no seawater intake and no brine discharge, (ii) a fully nature-powered mechanism directly driven by multiple renewable energy sources with zero usage of electricity, and (iii) a unique humidifier design using vertex-enhanced heat and mass transfer. The enabled desalination plant will be simple, robust, and environment-friendly, and is expected to produce freshwater in both large and small scales cost-effectively to meet diverse needs. Cost analysis and water quality analysis will be conducted in parallel with the technological advancement. The requested funds will be used to cover the expenses on: wages for three research assistants (graduate students), summer salary for three faculty members (the applicants), materials and supplies for the laboratory-scale prototype construction and water quality analysis, small instruments for testing the prototype, travel fees, and indirect costs. The proposed project will contribute to accomplishing the objectives 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 defined in Water Desalination Act of 1996 as amended by the Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation Act 0f 2016 and the objective 5 defined in Desalination 2008, as listed in page 1-2 of the FOA.

grant.title: Planning Grant: Engineering Research Center for Water Conservation/Management among Energy Industry, Agriculture, and Municipality
grant.abstract: The proposed ERC vision will be to develop a complete infrastructure for water conservation and management among energy industry, agriculture, and municipalities. There will be detailed water analysis on produced water and fracture fluid return from energy industry, water runoff from agriculture use, and greywater from municipality. The analysis will be summarized into a matrix that groups similar quality water products in order to generate a better perspective and overview of various water supplies. The next phase will be to employ various treatment strategies and determine the resulting water quality. These data will also be summarized in order to get a better perspective on achievements of each treatment technique. Based on literature review and detailed study on quality of water required for various applications (energy industry including petroleum (oil and gas), geothermal, agriculture, and municipality), a selection matrix will be developed on how the treated water can be utilized. A detailed study on the proximity of various industries will be conducted throughout the nation with emphasis on areas with greater density of oil and gas industry and agriculture. This analysis will indicate most optimal locations for synergy among the various stakeholders with greatest economical and societal impact. The impact of this water conservation/management on reduction of water disposal sites with possible contamination and seismic activities will be studied. In addition, the project will determine if there is a need to develop new technology or to combine existing treatment strategies in a new manner in order to achieve the required water quality given the influent water quality. Based on that determination, there might be work on developing those new methods to achieve the required objective. Furthermore, the quantity of water that can be conserved/managed among the various sectors nationwide will be determined, as that will measure the impact of this collaborative effort.

grant.title: Proposal to Establish a National Center for Integrated Transportation Infrastructure 4.0: Improving the Durability and Extending the Life of Transportation Infrastructure
grant.sponsor: U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) UTC Program
grant.abstract: This proposal establishes the Center for Integrated Transportation Infrastructure 4.0 (CITI-4.0), a National University Transportation Center focusing on “Improving the Durability and Extending the Life of Transportation Infrastructure”. CITI 4.0 is a consortium of seven US higher education and research institutions that consolidate their expertise, facilities, resources, and institutional support to achieve the common goals of the center. The center addresses the challenges of the new era Intelligent Transportation System in ways never previously imagined by adapting the “Industry 4.0” principles to the integrated transportation infrastructure. CITI-4.0 introduces automation, cyber-physical fusion and information driven practices, enabled by real-time data communications among heterogeneous monitoring sensors and integrates the assessment, management and maintenance activities of the infrastructure, resources and operations across railways, roadways, and ports following a data-driven performance-based approach. Motives: North America’s demand for safe, affordable, and environmentally responsible transportation of people and goods by railway, roadway, and ports is projected to grow substantially in the years ahead. Asset managers are consistently challenged to improve the performance of the transportation network, optimize efficiency of operations and ensure safety by maximizing accessibility and reliability of the transportation infrastructure. Although accurate monitoring is a key enabler for effective operations and maintenance, the condition assessment is currently conducted based mainly on periodic, labor-intensive and time-consuming scheduled activities. The interpretation of the collected data and integration with operations is extensively dependent on the experience of the operators and other human factors. Each transportation mode relies typically on its own operations, infrastructure, and resources to meet the current network demand. These three elements are often loosely integrated within each mode, are rarely integrated across modes, and are not effectively engaged with the end users of the network. Topic Areas: The center activities cover the following non-exclusive topics: (1) Application of new materials and technologies; (2) Cyber and communications security; (3) Condition monitoring, remote sensing, and the use of GPS; (4) Asset and performance management through data accessibility, data security and analytical tools; Impacts: CITI-4.0 brings the infrastructure of the major transportation modes into the Industry 4.0 era as essential parts of the grand Intelligent Transportation System. The proposed CITI-4.0 research, education, workforce development, technology transfer, and diversity activities advance technology in transportation engineering and enable students and professionals from diverse socioeconomic groups throughout the country to develop the skills necessary to overcome the transportation challenges of the next era and create the next generation of worldwide leaders. This initiative benefits all stakeholders in the transportation industry, administration and legislation and sets the framework for addressing similar problems around the world.

grant.abstract: There is a general lack of reliable data for the determination of the speciation and concentrations of arsenic and selenium in coal and fly-Ash. To address these limitations, we propose new experimental methods to perform a series of studies on coal and fly-Ash to determine the speciation and concentrations of arsenic and selenium. The work described in this proposal involves the acquisition of an in-house EXAFS system; an easyXAFS system. The combination of data collected from the easyXAFS system and an existing Thermo Scientific XPS system will be utilized to perform a series of studies on coal and fly- Ash to determine the speciation and concentrations of arsenic and selenium. The speciation studies will be utilized both in research and teaching. These studies will be utilized to train undergraduate students in XANES and XPS data collection and data analysis as it applies to coal and fly-ash analyses. Instrument will supplement the teaching curriculum in the chemistry and mechanical engineering departments at UTRGV. The overall objective of the proposed work is to develop a set of methods/techniques, for the utilization of in-house XAS and XPS to examine both the concentration and speciation of arsenic and selenium in coal and fly-ash samples. The PI and Co-PI will integrate XAS as a standard teaching and research tool at UTRGV in the chemical sciences and mechanical engineering. The acquisition of the easyXAFS system will provide for the training of approximately 60-80 minority STEM students (Hispanic students) per year, for the duration of the grant and for the lifetime of the instrument. This will be achieved through hands-on teaching with the instrument in courses offered in both, the Department of Chemistry and the Department of Mechanical Engineering at UTRGV. This training will better prepare UTRGV students to perform research and move forward in their careers as students or as professionals. The proposed work will provide a unique opportunity, to the students in the chemistry and mechanical engineering departments at UTRGV to carry out innovative research in the area characterization and determination of concentrations of arsenic and selenium in coal and fly-Ash. . This opportunity was only available to these students at a national laboratory.

grant.abstract: Project Summary: Recently, specifically engineered nanomaterials with controlled morphology continue to attract significant interest. Numerous scientific endeavors such as environmental remediation, dye sensitized solar cells (DSSCs), and battery technology benefit from the added development of synthetic strategies to design specific nano-architectures using composite materials. However, the relationships between synthesis, structure, and function are not well understood. This research hopes to uncover valuable information to further develop a better understanding of the links between synthesis, structure, and function in photoactive zinc oxide (ZnO) composite nanomaterials in photo-catalysis, molecular junctions in DSSCs, and as anode materials for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) and sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). To properly utilize ZnO’s photoactive properties for the aforementioned applications, we need to synthesize ZnO crystal structures composed of nanorods, nanowires, nanospheres, and nanosheets (consisting of hexagonal ZnO platelets). Composite materials consisting of these ZnO morphologies on graphene, graphene oxide, and reduced graphene oxide supports have the potential to photocatalytically degrade environmental contaminants such as atrazine, simazine, hexachlorophenol, and BPA. Additionally, we will examine the use of conductive organic thin films patterned with gold nanoparticles at the interface to serve as seed sites for the growth of ZnO nanowires for the preparation of molecular junctions in DSSCs.Finally, the synthesized ZnO/graphene, ZnO/graphene oxide, and ZnO/reduced graphene oxide composites are immobilized in polymer fibers through centrifugal spinning and converted into carbonized mats for application in structured zinc oxide/carbon composite anode materials for battery production.

grant.title: Design and Development: Transforming Underrepresented Minority Students Into Regional and National Engineering Innovators
grant.abstract: We propose a first program in a sequence that will address these issues. The focus of the proposed program will be on the development of critical non-technical skills on high school-to-freshman students as other programs already exist to address technical skills. The proposed intervention will promote the development of technical and non-technical skills through innovation experiences that aim to not only teach the principles of the innovation process, but also teach students how to transform themselves by applying said innovation principles. Engineering students collect a cumulus of STEM knowledge trusting and assuming that it will eventually become useful. It is common for engineering students to fail to connect their acquired knowledge to practical and relevant applications. Design and Innovation provides an excellent opportunity to make these connections by working on real-life regional challenges that provide a purpose to the learned knowledge and a motivation to become better students and professionals. Challenge Based Intruction (CBI) will be used as the pedagogical approach to present these innovation experiences to the students. CBI has proven to help students develop adaptive expertise, which in this case is key to not only create an innovation or learn the innovation process, but also apply innovation to self. These innovation experiences will be calibrated by first evaluating incoming high school students to identify their technical and non-technical deficiencies and re-evaluating to see how these skills are being developed after the proposed interventions. Initially it won’t be feasible to include every single incoming engineering student in the proposed program; our aim is to intervene a selected group to create a critical mass of transformed innovator students that can have an initial impact on their classroom communities. These students will lead communities of learning and take other initiatives that will help disseminate innovation thinking, serve as models and motivate other non-participating students. Future programs will focus on a sequence of increasingly complex innovation experiences through sophomore, junior and senior years aimed at developing self as a student, as a professional and as an innovator. Our overarching goal is to prepare professional engineers that can help in the development of the RGV region by generating their own opportunities for innovation.

grant.title: Proposal to Establish a UTRGV/STC NSF Resource Hub
grant.abstract: PROJECT OVERVIEW On August 31, 2015, The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) opened its doors as one of the first universities of the 21st Century and the second largest Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI) in the nation. UTRGV’s Fall enrollment was 27,809 students in which 89% were Hispanic/Latino and 88.5% were in undergraduate classes. South Texas College (STC), a HSI, founded in 1993 is accredited to award four (4) baccalaureate degrees and 119 associate degrees. More than 34,000 students attend STC at their five state- of-the-art campuses, two teaching centers, and one virtual campus. UTRGV and STC in response to the Congressional Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2017 and the American Innovation and Competitiveness Act through the NSF Improving Undergraduate STEM Education – HSI Program propose the following goal and objectives: Project goal is to create the UTRGV/STC HSI STEM Resource Hub with three Leadership Institutes to build capacity and improve the quality of the undergraduate (associate or baccalaureate) experience, increase retention and graduation at HSIs with little to no prior NSF funding in order to produce a more qualified, innovative, and diverse STEM workforce. Objective #1 – Create and Implement the Critical Transitions Leadership Institute focusing on the development of new knowledge about successful advancement of undergraduates at HSIs through critical transitions, including the transition from lower-division to upper-division coursework. Objective #2 – Create and Implement the Cross-Sector Partnerships Leadership Institute that establishes projects that develop mutually beneficial partnerships to build faculty capacity and student opportunities to conduct STEM research or STEM education research at HSIs. Project services will include NSF Proposal writing and financial compliance training, in addition to facilitating networking and professional development opportunities that build and strengthen collaborations among HSIs. Objective #3 – Create and Implement the Research on Broadening Participation in STEM Leadership Institute that will generate new knowledge about how to enhance undergraduate STEM education that results in an increase in retention and graduation rates of undergraduate students pursuing degrees in STEM fields at HSIs. INTELLECTUAL MERIT New knowledge will be added through the UTRGV/STC HSI STEM Resource Hub’s project services and activities. The planned activities will result in an increase in Hispanic participation in STEM fields, in research, conferences, professional associations, and future leadership. In addition, there will be an increase in research and education opportunities for HSI faculty and students created through collaborations across participating HSIs. Successful research grant submissions will lead to increased research participation from HSIs. Increases will be documented in foundational and exploratory research, design and development research, and impact research from an underrepresented population. Developing faculty and administrators to use the best practices of transitioning students from secondary to post-secondary, 2-year to 4-year institutions, and on to graduate programs incorporating pedagogical practices, curriculum development, teacher and faculty development, and NSF research grant funding, then applying research into learning and education. New knowledge of educational best practices of successful Hispanic student transition and faculty support mechanisms will be identified through the project data evaluation and assessment process. BROADER IMPACTS Enhance the capabilities of students, faculty, and administrative leaders to take advantage of opportunities and develop solutions that improve the quality of undergraduate STEM education at their institutions. Through improving the undergraduate experience at HSIs, there will be an increase in student enrollment, student retention rates, and graduation rates in STEM programs. Increased access for HSI groups to the Nations STEM Enterprise. Increased research and education grant submissions to NSF grant programs from HSIs. Ultimately, the success of this project will produce a more qualified, innovative, and diverse STEM workforce. Facilitate development of partnerships that encourage the sharing of resources and facilities among HSIs and other institutions that will result in more competitive proposal submissions to NSF among other federal, industry, state, and local government agencies focused on enhancing STEM education.

grant.title: An engineered hydrologic cycle for fresh water from oceans
grant.abstract: Two-thirds of the world’s population face severe water scarcity (Sci. Adv. 2, e1500323, ’16). Existing desalination technologies (e.g., membrane-based, thermal-based, etc.) have various drawbacks on scale up, energy consumption, water quality, and environmental impact (Water Res., 75, 164, ’15). Emerging technologies for collection of airborne water are limited to small-scale production (Science, 356, 430, ’17). Mother Nature feeds the globe with freshwater by extracting it from oceans through the hydrologic cycle (HC) – evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. We propose an engineering research project to engineer the HC at an ocean site for utility-scale freshwater production. Simply put, moist warm air over the ocean surface continuously enters a downward flow passage and reaches a certain water depth, where the air is naturally cooled by chilled ocean water and the airborne water is collected through condensation. The cold dry air then runs through an upward flow passage, escapes at the warm ocean surface, and recovers temperature and humidity. The uniqueness is on realizing a fully nature-powered engineered HC: winds to feed the site with inexhaustible moisture-laden air, waves to drive the air through the flow passage, the temperature gradient of the ocean water to provide cooling for condensation, and the solar energy to power humidity replenishment.

grant.title: Development, Characterization, and Modeling of Multi-Layer Fabric Reinforced with Shear-Thickening Fluids Created with Sub-Micron Silica and Soda-Lime Glass Particles
grant.abstract: Researchers at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) have developed patent pending technologies to convert waste glass into single-digit micron and sub-micron (300±200 nanometers) glass particles that have unique properties not found in bulk glass. Waste glass is typical soda lime glass with about 60-90% silica and 40-10% other (sodium, calcium, and aluminum) oxides. The principal investigators (PIs) at UTRGV have found that the properties of recycled glass fine particles that have been processed into superfine particles are dramatically different. The PIs are interested in understanding the myriad of processing-property-microstructure relationships of these glass particles and composites (i.e., multi-layer fabric reinforced with shear thickening fluids made from these particles). The basic science research component of this DoD project will initially concentrate on submicron silica or glass particles by themselves to define and demonstrate systematically the underlying processing-property-microstructure relationships, and their controlled manipulation under dynamic conditions to create the next generation composites for superior performance. Modeling efforts will include experimentally informed and validated finite element analysis. After gaining a thorough insight into each type of particle, the study will be extended to the combination of micron and submicron silica and glass particles. The soda-lime glass fine particles can be commercially produced from waste glass for under a dollar (target price) a pound, which also has a positive impact on the environment through recycling. Equally relevant is the fact that it is foreseen that these submicron glass particles can be produced in commercial quantities of tens of tons per day. These new materials and derived material systems and their properties have a great potential to address key Department of Defense, ARMY Research Office (ARO) interests. Specifically, (a) detailed understanding of complex material system behavior and its capability during service, and (b) to utilize material’s capabilities close to their limiting capacity (ARO, Solid Mechanics - Understanding of Mechanical Behavior of Complex Material Systems). grant.title: Energy transfer between waves and a vertical-axis unidirectional rotor
grant.abstract: This proposed research into harvesting ocean wave energy will optimize the efficiency of wave energy converters (WECs) thereby bringing them closer in line to other renewable energy sources. At present, there is a global effort to strive for alternative, sustainable, energy sources. The oceans are a huge reservoir of constantly renewing energy carried by ocean waves. This energy source, known as "Blue Energy," has been largely untapped. If funded, this project will make a huge impact in our ability to harvest this resource. The main objective of the proposed work is to gain a fundamental understanding of the energy transfer process between waves and a WEC. The constantly changing nature of water flow in waves requires that efficient energy conversion occur for all possible flow directions in a dynamic fashion. The research findings of this work will lay the foundation for WEC development and provide an experimentally-verified theoretical framework that will enable the creation of efficient WEC devices that maximize wave-to-WEC energy transfer and minimize the reverse. A novel class of WECs, originated and validated by the PI, will be the focus of the work. These WEC have a rotor performing unidirectional rotation about a vertical axis in waves; that is in contrast to reciprocating motion of most other WEC technologies. The rotor can have various types of blades (e.g. hydrofoil or hemispherical) that interact with the waves to produce unidirectional motion. The wave-rotor interaction will be studied experimentally for different types of blades using a laboratory wave flume, and theoretically using both detailed computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling and intuitive phenomenological modeling techniques. All three approaches will be compared so that a full understanding of the wave-rotor interaction will be obtained. Using this proposed research as a platform, a new model of engineering education will be demonstrated between two Hispanic-serving institutions through cross-border (U.S. and Mexico) collaborations.

grant.title: Engineering Transportation Research in STEM Fields
grant.sponsor: National Science Foundation (NSF) RET Site Program
grant.abstract: Project Summary 1. Overview: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and its University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) aim to establish a new Engineering RET Site entitled: “Transportation Engineering Research in STEM Fields.” Since transportation engineering is an interdisciplinary field, the teachers will be exposed to research projects from mechanical, electrical, civil, and manufacturing and industrial engineering disciplines. UTRGV and UTCRS will partner with South Texas College (STC), La Joya Independent School District, and Pharr-San Juan-Alamo Independent School District. STC is the largest Hispanic serving community college in the nation with over 34,000 students, of whom 70% are first generation college goers, over 95% are Hispanic, and greater than 75% are on financial aid. La Joya ISD is the fourth largest school district in the Lower Rio Grande Valley and home to 30,000 PreK-12 students (99.7% Hispanic) and 2,035 teachers. PSJA ISD is home to 32,600 K-12 students (99% Hispanic) and over 2200 teachers. Both La Joya ISD and PSJA ISD are among the highest poverty rates in the U.S. Ten STEM teachers and faculty will be recruited annually from STC, PSJA ISD, and La Joya ISD to participate in the proposed RET program. The teachers/faculty will spend ten weeks per year as part of their involvement in the RET Program. Six of the ten weeks will be spent on the UTRGV campus during the summer, and the remaining four weeks will be effort expended during the academic year developing and implementing modules and interactive hands-on activities in STEM classrooms, and presentations to other teachers in organized STEM teacher workshops and symposiums. Constantine Tarawneh, Principal Investigator, Ph. (956) 867-5907, constantine.tarawneh@utrgv.edu, will serve as the point-of-contact for teacher/faculty recruitment. The RET Site will utilize the existing UTCRS web site http://railwaysafety.utrgv.edu/. Key Words: transportation engineering research, railway safety, bearing condition monitoring, advanced sensor technologies, STEM teacher workshops and symposiums, STEM teaching modules. 2. Intellectual Merit: The proposed UTRGV RET Site is different from any of the previously NSF funded sites in that it focuses on transportation engineering research as an interdisciplinary field of study encompassing mechanical, electrical, civil, and manufacturing and industrial engineering. There has been only one transportation related site previously funded through NSF entitled: “Innovative Transportation Systems,” which focused on transportation solutions in rural areas. The new proposed RET Site will introduce faculty and teachers to a broad range of transportation engineering research in areas such as advanced bearing condition monitoring techniques, proactive maintenance cycles for railroad rolling stock, advanced sensor technologies, advanced materials research, and intelligent control systems. The UTCRS is one of only two rail-focused USDOT centers under their UTC Program, and has a very well-established track record of research in this field engaging faculty, students, and teachers from different disciplines to solve interdisciplinary transportation engineering problems. The teachers/faculty will be seamlessly integrated with the ongoing research teams and will work on preparing grade-level appropriate teaching and research modules that the faculty/teachers can implement in their respective STEM classrooms. UTRGV and UTCRS faculty and students will assist the RET teachers/faculty in the implementation process, and will provide year-long oversight, supervision, and assessment and evaluation. 3. Broader Impacts: Beyond Traffic: 2045 Final Report [1] issued by the USDOT in response to the transportation FAST Act bill clearly outlines the need to raise awareness about transportation fields across the nation. As current leaders in the transportation industry near retirement, it is imperative that we cultivate the next generation of highly-skilled workforce that will deliver our twenty-first century transportation infrastructure. The proposed RET Site aims at working hand-in-hand with our teachers/faculty to bring transportation engineering into K-16 classrooms with the purpose of motivating and exciting historically underrepresented students to pursue careers in this interdisciplinary field to meet the needs of the aging transportation workforce.

grant.title: ISRP: A self-sustaining process to get fresh water from oceans
grant.sponsor: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.sponsor_type: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: The project aims to explore a new process to get fresh water from oceans. The process is to be fully powered by the oceans themselves by means of the temperature gradient and waves. It does not use membranes to desalinate seawater. It does not produce brine either. Rather, it mimics the earth’s hydrologic cycle to a certain extent. Specifically, above an ocean surface warm air gains high humidity through natural solar heating. Below the ocean surface the water temperature naturally decreases with increasing water depth. By forcing the moisture-laden warm air to circulate through a cooling path down to the cold ocean at a certain depth, condensation occurs and fresh water is collected. The air circulation is driven by ocean waves. With the help of winds, inexhaustible moisture-laden air can continuously move into the dehumidification site, making large-scale fresh water production possible.
