grant.title: Prototyping and Testing of Electrically Conductive Thermoplastic Poyurethane Railroad Suspension Pad
grant.sponsor: University Transportation Center for Railroad Safety
grant.abstract: This research will take formulations of carbon nanofibers in thermoplastic polyurethanes (TPU), which have shown promising levels of electric conductivity, for use in a conductive steering pad, and prepare them for deployment in a commercially viable product. Plain elastomers are insulators and prevent transmission of current from rail to frame to signal door or gate opening devices. In addition, the thermal insulating properties of these materials reduce the rate of heat flow from bearings through the bearing adapter and into the side-frame, where it can be dissipated. Previous studies performed by the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) revealed that traditional conductive additives, such as carbon black, must be applied at high volume fraction in order to generate sufficient conductivity, which in turn results in substantial increases in pad stiffness and degradation of pad durability. Vapor Grown Carbon Nanofibers (VGCNF) are extremely efficient conductive additives that can produce the desired conductivity at much lower concentrations and with less impact on mechanical performance than traditional additives. Prior efforts have identified a TPU carbon nanofiber combination and fiber loading that produces excellent conductivity, and results in an electrically conductive part when molded under commercially useful molding temperatures. The identified system first needs to be scaled from laboratory quantity testing to injection molding quantities, and then prototyped. Moreover, the microstructural contributions to conductivity as well as the allowable processing range need to be fully described in order to support process development and quality control processes in commercialization.

Synthesis, processing and characterization of novel hyper organic/inorganic materials for catalytic applications
grant.abstract: Alumina (Al2O3) is widely used as catalyst support media in the Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) processes of crude oil due to its textural properties such as surface area and their acid/base characteristics. However, the chemical and hydrothermal stability of Al2O3 are still a critical point for catalytic applications due to many challenges, which may block the active sites of the catalyst resulting in catalyst instability. Strategies for minimizing these problems have involved the use of carbon, TiO2, silica and carbon nanotubes as alternative catalyst supports due to their high surface area, strong metal support interaction, and acid-base properties. This proposal involves the use of Forcespinning (FS) of a high melting point polymer to fabricate polymer/ceramic composite fibers as a catalyst support in heterogeneous catalysis. Unlike traditionally extruded supported catalysts, the polymer forcespun-supported catalysts should have lighter weights, better packing resulting in longer life times for the catalysts. The better packing will result from the packing of polymer nonwoven mats into the catalytic beds instead of extruded cylindrical based pellets. The current proposal focuses on establishing a fundamental understanding of the relationships between processing, structure, composition, and performance of polymer fibers to improve the manufacturability of the material and to understand how the interaction between the polymer fibers and catalyst nanoparticles. Successful demonstration of the proposed work will lead to new fabrication methods for polymer-supported catalyst that extend the catalysis operational range beyond its current capabilities and will provide a significant advancement in understanding the behavior of catalyst support materials under operating conditions.

grant.title: The synthesis and design of a new system of Ionic Liquid Electrolytes for Lithium ion Batteries
grant.sponsor_type: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: This project aims to develop Ionic Liquid based electrolytes for use in Lithium-ion batteries. As we move away from energy produced from fossil fuels to those produced from renewable sources, such as solar energy and wind energy, energy storage is becoming an important problem that needs to be addressed in order for these sources to be more widely used. Batteries used for energy storage consist of a positive electrode, a negative electrode, and an electrolyte solution which allows the movement of positively and negatively charged ions (cations and anions) between the electrodes. Currently, Lithium-ion batteries are the most widely used batteries. One major limitation in further developing these batteries, is the current use of volatile, flammable and toxic compounds in the electrolyte medium. By developing new Ionic Liquids, we aim to gain a better understanding of the properties of Ionic Liquids, and develop better and safer batteries. The results of the study will be used for external grant applications and will be published in peer-reviewed journals and presented in national and international conferences.

USDOT University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS): Improving the Durability and Extending the Life of Transportation Infrastructure
grant.sponsor: U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) UTC Program
grant.abstract: The proposed US DOT University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) will deploy research teams focused on improving the durability and extending the life of railway transportation systems within the United States. Informed by state-of-the-art safety data reporting and management paradigms, the UTCRS teams will concentrate their research efforts in the following areas: • Improving durability and extending the life of safety-critical components of rolling stock, including draw-gear, axles, wheels, and bearings; • Increasing durability and extending the life of rail with a focus on reducing the potential for broken rail under service; • Improving durability and extending the life of rail support systems, including cross tie systems, ballast systems, and base and sub-base foundational systems; • Increasing durability and extending the life of railway bridge structures via an integrated systems approach to modeling, design, construction, inspection, and maintenance that includes strategic cyber-infrastructure systems technology development and deployment; • Investigate and develop strategic engineered system asset and performance management technologies; • Investigate and develop railway construction process methodologies and railway construction and maintenance management systems that lead to improved product outcomes in terms of durability and fault-free service life; and • Identify and investigate technology that increases opportunities for railway transportation to increase the durability, life, and safety of highway transportation through strategic shifting of freight haul services. Aging Infrastructure: An Integrated Systems Approach to Improving Railway Transportation Systems It is increasingly understood that the disparate physical aspects of railway transportation systems cannot be treated separately, but must in reality be modeled, designed, inspected, and maintained as integrated systems and systems of systems. Each asset and its constituent components can and does affect the performance of interfacing assets and their components. For example, the rails interact in a very complex manner with the wheels, bearings, and axles of the rolling stock. Furthermore, the rails interact with the track structure foundational elements (ties, ballast, base and sub-base) in a very complex and time-, temperature-, moisture-, and load-dependent and evolutionary manner over the life of the railway. Unfortunately, it has not been customary in the past to treat these interfaced components as integrated systems. Guided by cutting-edge systems-of-systems research principles, the UTCRS research teams will directly address the co-dependencies and mutual dependencies within and among the assets upon which safe and reliable railway transportation depends.

MRI: Acquisition of subsystems to upgrade an existing planar PIV to a tomographic PIV for multidisciplinary research and education
grant.abstract: This proposal is for acquisition of subsystems to upgrade a previously-acquired planar (2D) Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) system to a tomographic (3D) PIV. Such an upgrade is commercially available; no further development effort is needed. PIV is an optical method to measure instantaneous velocity fields and other properties in fluids. Due to the highly modular structure, the upgraded PIV system will allow easy interchange between 2D velocimetry (the existing function) and 3D velocimetry (the augmented function). This proposed new 3D PIV system will support multidisciplinary research of four faculty members from two departments at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB). Four research areas, two in mechanical engineering and two in environmental sciences, will be greatly facilitated by the 3D PIV. The four areas include energy harvesting from ocean waves, flow-cylinder interaction, interchange of salinity in mixing flows in an estuary, and water quality study. To take full advantage of this state-of-the-art instrument, a PIV club for broadened research training will be formed, and a 3D PIV demonstration experiment for an undergraduate lab course will be developed. A systematic approach will be to use the PIV demonstration as a forerunner and the PIV club as a bridge to integrate all the PIV-enabled research with education in both science and engineering at UTB (a minority-serving institution).

grant.abstract: We propose a solution to kill two birds with one stone: develop a morphing wing for drones to ride winds and save battery life. We will mimic bat wings to achieve desired aerodynamic performance through a simple, light, and easy-to-maneuver mechanical design; artificial muscle fibers will replace traditional motors for actuation. We vision that the drone can extend its wings to glide like a bird when wind is favorable. When wind is not favorable, the wings will be stretched in. With increased flight time, small drones are suitable for real world applications. Furthermore, we propose to enable the intelligence of drones by developing algorithms in computer vision, target recognition and multi-agent collaborative learning. Our goal is to explore the low space (<400m altitude) where we see countless applications directly benefiting human life: photography, transportation, surveillance, etc.

grant.title: RUI: Hydrodynamic characterization of a rotor in waves for unidirectional rotary motion
grant.abstract: This RUI project contributes to energy harvesting from ocean waves by advancing knowledge in hydrodynamics of a wave-driven rotor. Ocean waves can directly drive wave energy converters (WECs) to perform two types of motion – reciprocating motion and unidirectional rotary motion. In general, the efficiency of a reciprocating WEC is strongly wave-frequency dependent, whereas the efficiency of a rotary WEC can be somewhat wave-frequency independent. To date, a huge majority of WEC technologies under development in industry belong to the reciprocating class, whereas only a few WEC concepts fall in the unidirectional rotary class. In this research, a new wave-driven rotor for unidirectional rotary motion is proposed. To characterize the rotor performance and gain fundamental understanding of wave-rotor interaction, a systematic experimental study will be conducted in a wave tank. Multiple experimental methods (particle image velocimetry [PIV], hot film anemometry [HFA], loading cells, and accelerometers) will be employed to reveal the flow physics from different perspectives. To integrate this wave energy research with undergraduate education, a bench-scale rotor-equipped WEC will be iteratively developed by a large number of undergraduate students in parallel with, and guided by, the hydrodynamic research. Specifically, students will contribute to the prototype WEC development by doing WEC-related design projects which will be implemented in a series of engineering courses.

CAREER: Wave interaction with a direct-drive rotor for unidirectional rotary motion
grant.abstract: This CAREER project contributes to energy harvesting from ocean waves by advancing the knowledge of wave interaction with a direct-drive rotor. Ocean waves can directly drive wave energy converters (WECs) to perform two types of motion – reciprocating motion and unidirectional rotary motion. Analysis shows that unidirectional rotary motion is advantageous over reciprocating motion in achieving high efficiency. However, a huge majority of WEC concepts/technologies belong to the reciprocating class. Only a very few concepts have been presented—but no actual technologies have ever been developed—in the unidirectional rotary class. In this research, a direct-drive rotor is proposed to realize unidirectional rotary motion in waves. To gain fundamental understanding of wave-rotor interaction, a systematic experimental study will be conducted in a wave tank. A rotor with simple blades (cylindrical shells of semicircular cross section) will be explored at different degrees of freedom and under a wide range of wave and rotor parameters. Multiple experimental methods (particle image velocimetry [PIV], hot film anemometry [HFA], loading cells, and accelerometers) will be employed to reveal the flow physics from different perspectives. In addition, a bench-scale rotor-instrumented WEC will be iteratively developed in parallel with, and guided by, the wave-rotor interaction research. This WEC development is intended to create a platform that promotes integration of research and education in multiple schemes under the theme of wave energy harvesting; it is all to be accomplished by undergraduate students.

grant.title: Collaborative Research: A fully-shielded and free-floating wave energy converter with low maintenance demand
grant.abstract: This research proposes an innovative wave energy converter (WEC) architecture for energy harvesting from ocean waves. The proposed WEC is free-floating over the ocean surface and converts the wave motion to electricity. The scavenged electricity is transmitted to a nearby base station wirelessly, and then delivered to an onshore power station via an undersea cable. The proposed WEC is fully-shielded and hence is free from seawater corrosion. In addition, it employs a highly-robust wave-riding mechanism. As a result, it requires little maintenance for at least five years. Its success is expected to significantly lower the high maintenance cost associated with wave energy harvesting. The objective of this research is to verify the feasibility of the proposed WEC architecture. It includes the following three major tasks. Task A: To study the hydrodynamic characteristics of free-floating and fully-sealed WECs comprehensively. Task B: To investigate efficient wireless power transmission schemes between a wave-riding WEC and a stationary base station, by taking advantage of novel radar technology to construct highly-directional wireless channels dynamically. Task C: To realize an integrated WEC prototype and demonstrate its performance in a wave tank. This interdisciplinary project will be carried out collaboratively by three investigators — two from mechanical engineering and one from electrical engineering. One expert from the offshore energy industry will serve as the consultant in our team.

NSF-MRI: Acquisition of Micro Particle Velocimetry (micro-PIV) System for Microfluidics and Biomedical Applications
grant.abstract: PROJECT SUMMARY This proposal is for the acquisition of a Micro-Particle Image Velocimetry (micro-PIV) system to conduct micro-fluidics, MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical-systems), and biomedical flow experiments for both research and student training at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB). UTB is a minority-serving institution in the Rio Grande Valley (RGV) of Texas. With a population of 1.5 million, comprised primarily of Hispanics, the RGV is the fourth-largest populated region in the state. UTB is the only institution in the RGV that offers both engineering physics and engineering technology programs. The RGV, a historically underrepresented region, presently has no micro-PIV systems to support science and engineering students. The MRI investment would provide promising young investigators with the resources required to greatly raise the stature of research in the RGV, attract new sources of research support, and elevate MEMS and biomedical education for Hispanic students to a competitive level. Intellectual Merit The project supports four specific research components detailed in this proposal. The titles and intellectual merits of these research activities are as follows: (i) Integration of Microcantilever with AC Electrokinetics for Sensing Bio-/Nano-Particles. This activity will result in an improved fundamental understanding of the AC Electrokinetics mechanism in complex electrode patterns and sensing bio-/nano-particles. Experiments using the micro-PIV system will further the understanding of electrochemistry at electrode/electrolyte interfaces in non-uniform AC fields and the interplay between bioparticles and AC electric fields for the implementation of high-efficiency bioparticle collection and separation. (ii) Biased AC Electroosmosis Micropump for Water Management in PEM Fuel Cells. This activity will use the micro-PIV system in research related to vortices in novel biased AC electroosmotic micropumps. This fundamental study is important to understanding fluid mixing and enhancing the efficiency of pumping in micro-channels. (iii) Biomimetic Flow Sensing. The main objective of this activity is to obtain the micro-scale time-dependent flow structures, and to correlate them with a canal Biomimetic Neuromast (BN) response under comparable conditions. (iv) Selective Filtration/Absorption of Nano- and Micron- Size Particles Using Carbon Nanotube-Based Media. This activity will synthesize carbon nanotube-based media with various morphologies and densities to selectively filter nano- and micron-size particles from fluid flow. Major advances will mainly depend on finding solutions to multidisciplinary research areas. The broader impact of the proposed research activities stems from the infrastructure enhancement that the micro-PIV system acquisition would mean to the MEMS and biomimetic laboratory of the UTB Engineering Department. The acquisition would support current research projects and supplement some of our existing advanced equipment, resulting in more efficient and effective use. The proposed project will prepare qualified, skilled graduate and undergraduate students interested in multidisciplinary research. The PIs will engage undergraduate/graduate students in research and thesis projects. Academic enrichment includes student training based on investigation and characterization of interdisciplinary class projects. One of the objectives for the student training is to encourage undergraduate/graduate students to continue their doctoral studies at appropriate institutions. Because a large percentage of women in the RGV lack a college diploma in science and engineering, women from the local, underrepresented Hispanic population will be recruited to become researchers. The project will help to improve measurement and instrumentation skills while introducing students to exciting research areas in MEMS design, micro-fluidics and biomimetics. The micro-PIV system will be used to demonstrate fluid flow in micropumps and to analyze data in MEMS/biological sensors for NSF-REU; and to provide research exposure for visiting summer high school students, motivating them to choose careers in science and engineering. Faculty discussions related to the proposed micro-PIV system and its use have fostered growing interest from other fields, particularly biological sciences. This project has great potential for interdisciplinary research and collaboration. The project will enhance UTB’s research program and will be available for up to 20 students’ senior design and thesis research projects within the next five years. Classification: UTB is a non-Ph.D.-granting institution and a minority-serving university.

grant.abstract: This prospectus is offered in support of establishing the US DOT University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS). The UTCRS comprises a consortium of three universities: The University of Texas - Pan American, Edinburg, Texas (UTPA); Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas (TAMU); and The University of Nebraska - Lincoln, Lincoln, Nebraska (UNL). The UTCRS will develop knowledge, diverse human resources, and innovative technology in support of strategic safety plans for the U.S. rail transportation industry. The center will engage and focus its partners’ established expertise and leverage and expand their existing resources to establish comprehensive programs of rail safety research, education, technology transfer and implementation, and workforce development. The UTCRS aims to reduce the number of accidents and equipment failures experienced in rail transportation systems. This will result directly in reduced fatalities and injuries in addition to reduced economic losses to stakeholders. New technology and associated workforce development will lead to improved safety assessments, safety counter measures, decision-making tools, and greater long-term safety gains.

grant.title: RUI: Wave-energy-converter pitch dynamics and its coupling with heave and surge
grant.abstract: We propose to advance the exploration in wave-energy-convertor (WEC) hydrodynamics by focusing on wave interaction with WECs. A WEC is a general means used to harvest energy from ocean waves. The overall objective of this project is to better understand the flow physics of the nonlinear wave interaction with free-floating WECs. The fundamental understanding gained will guide the development of a proof-of-concept WEC that: (i) uses angular oscillation (pitch) to harvest wave energy, and (ii) demonstrates the potential to generate low-cost electricity. In this project, we will integrate research with undergraduate education. Five research tasks and three education tasks will be carried out in parallel throughout the duration of this project. The research aspect of this project has a focus on WEC hydrodynamics that is to be conducted experimentally in a wave tank. The education component involves participation of both undergraduate and local high-school students and improvement of our engineering curriculum.

grant.title: SEP Collaborative: A system to harvest wave energy for low-cost electricity
grant.abstract: This research proposes an innovative approach for energy harvesting from ocean waves at a low cost. It employs brand-new wave farm architecture, in which free-floating and fully-encapsulated wave energy convertors (WECs) are deployed in the ocean around a base station. The WECs convert wave energy into electricity. The scavenged electricity is transmitted to the base station wirelessly and then delivered from the base station to an onshore power station via an undersea cable. The major objective of this research is to achieve WECs that can be easily deployed and that demand little maintenance in a lifespan of about six years. Its success is expected to significantly lower the costs associated with wave energy scavenging, and further, to promote ocean waves as a competitive renewable energy source. This interdisciplinary project will be carried out collaboratively by five PIs, one senior personnel, and one industrial consultant.

grant.title: Multimodal Modules for Inquiry-Based Statics and Dynamics Curriculum
grant.abstract: This project will develop multimodal Engineering Mechanics modules (i.e. incorporating multiple modes of physical or virtual interaction) designed to teach concepts through experimentation to students with limited Calculus and Physics proficiency. The modules will serve three audiences: 1. Undergraduate engineering majors who struggle to conceptualize Engineering Mechanics, 2. Non-engineering undergraduates seeking a technical minor or associates degree,1 and 3. High-school students learning basic Mechanics in Mathematics and Science courses. Students struggle to conceptualize Engineering Mechanics (i.e. Newtonian Physics, Statics, and Dynamics) fundamentals because they cannot effectively visualize the effects of external loads on physical systems and/or do not intuitively comprehend the static or dynamic response [1]. Traditionally, Engineering Mechanics courses have been primarily lecture-based with little experimentation. The PIs contend that through the use of simple bench-top experiments or virtual representations of physical systems, students, especially those who underperform or show limited proficiency in Calculus and Physics, can more effectively interpret concepts. Furthermore, such tools are more effective at overcoming common misconceptions. INTELLECTUAL MERIT: The multimodal modules will be designed to encourage properly conceived understanding of fundamentals through discovery and experience to better address common misconceptions. The modules will engender proper engineering intuition and critical thinking by forcing students to discover and identify the underlying principles. The focus will be more on facilitating development of qualitative analysis and less on quantitative problem solving skills. This project will formally and exhaustively assess the impact of using multimodal curriculum to (1) dispel common Engineering Mechanics misconceptions and (2) enable students with limited proficiency in the underlying Mathematics and Physics. The multimodal modules will be based, in part, on modules previously developed and piloted at The University of Texas-Pan American (UTPA) with the support of seed money from the Mechanical Engineering Department. BROADER IMPACT: The modules will also be tested at the South Texas College (STC), a regional community college, and at South Texas Independent School District’s Business, Education, and Technology Academy (b ETA), a local school serving grades 7-12. At UTPA the modules will be used for engineering majors, technology related minors, and K-12 students participating in summer programs. The modules will be organized into a comprehensive series that will be readily scalable to the various target audiences. Successful development, implementation, and evaluation will enable widespread use of such modules at other institutions and in other disciplines. Less than 10%of entering freshman at UTPA begin their Math sequence in Calculus I or higher. This generates a significant delay till students are eligible to take entry level Engineering courses or even prerequisites, which threatens the retention of first-year Engineering students. To combat this, an Introduction to Engineering course with no Math or Physics prerequisites is offered to all students and is a first-year requirement for Engineering majors. Using multimodal modules in early courses such as this and throughout the Engineering Mechanics sequence will preempt misconceptions and reinforce properly founded understanding. The modules can replace specific homework assignments or lectures.

Pilot and feasibility Study: Investigation for the establishment of a challenge based mobile informal learning platform to explore STEM concepts in ergonomics, biomechanics, and work physiology
grant.abstract: The proposed approach will be to integrate STEM concepts associated with human performance facilitating interactive methodology in the development of the proposed informal learning system. In this first pilot, the work will focus on integrating concepts and technologies related to ergonomics, biomechanics, and work physiology together with challenge-based instruction educational design, and affordable mobile laboratory technologies. Examples of the technologies to be included are motion capture using very affordable and transportable off the shelf equipment such as KINECT and open-source motion capture software, and a wireless, high quality, 3D manipulation sensor with software applications. The final results of the project will be a pilot challenge based mobile informal learning platform system that will support the execution of an implementation plan throughout the Rio Grande Valley in South Texas as a test bed. This will include an outreach strategy to local museums, community centers, afterschool programs, school districts and other appropriate venues to ensure the establishment of the informal learning environment. In addition, the plan will include an assessment of the educational value and impact of the system in terms of learning for both students and parents as it relates to the project target STEM fields. If successful, the expectation is that the results will provide useful information that will lead the PI and team to formulate potential additional Research in Service to Practice, Innovations in Development, or Broad Implementation proposals. This is precisely the fundamental premise behind the pilot program category of programs which is to produce evidence, findings, and/or prototype deliverables that help the team make critical decisions about future work

grant.title: Training Engineers as Resilient Innovators for the RGV Region and the Nation
grant.sponsor: P&G Fund US Higher Education Grant Program
grant.abstract: We propose the creation of the “League of Extraordinary Innovators”, an extracurricular innovation clinic to provide students with a micro-experience on technical innovation that includes problem identification, product design, product realization, and entrepreneurship. Teams of undergraduate students from all engineering departments and levels will submit an application. Teams will be encouraged to address regional needs with their technical solutions, such as educational toys, extremely affordable prosthetics, etc. Selected teams will be coached and supported through the 2-month experience having to go through periodical reviews similar to “shark tanks” where they will receive crucial feedback. A multidisciplinary faculty group will provide advice to the teams. Students will receive a small budget and access to the Mechanical Engineering Senior Design Lab to work on their prototypes. At the end of each program (Spring and Fall), each team must present: a prototype of their product, a canvas business model, a completed Intellectual Property disclosure form, and a completed application to a national or regional design, venture or student competition. The teams will be evaluated on various metrics, for example: multidisciplinary collaboration, creativity of ideas, design effectiveness, implementation of STEM knowledge, new knowledge acquisition, social and environmental impact, etc. Our objective is to engage the engineering student community, create a culture of innovation that instills confidence and assertiveness in our students and provides a real-life application context for STEM knowledge. The U.S., specially our Rio Grande Valley (RGV) region requires resilient innovators capable of creating opportunities in a nascent entrepreneurial ecosystem. The non-traditional nature of the program promotes a learning environment that encourages students to take risks necessary for innovation, deal with failure and develop resiliency skills.

US-Peru Study Abroad Program: Training Engineers as Resilient Innovators
grant.sponsor: 100,000 Strong in the Americas Innovation Fund
grant.abstract: How can we effectively train our students to be successful in an ever-changing world? On one hand we have great scientific and technological discoveries and on the other a growing list of challenges such as poverty, hunger, limited access to clean water, among others (UN Sustainable Goals). Our region, country and world require resilient innovators that can create opportunities as independent entrepreneurs, or as part of industry, business or a local community organization. We must train our students to become agents of change, applying their STEAM knowledge to provide technical solutions to solve society’s problems. Design challenges can provide a motivational, engaging, comprehensive, and realistic context for students to apply their knowledge and to understand the sustainability of a solution. Sustainability in this case has a broader sense and includes not only technical feasibility, but also ethical implications, sociocultural impact, financial structure, IP protection, and environmental impact, among other considerations. For this reason, we propose the US-Peru Study Abroad Program: Training Students as Resilient Innovators between the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and the Universidad Nacional de Ingenieria (UNI) in Lima, Peru. In essence this program will provide a “micro-entrepreneurship” experience with service learning projects in the Rio Grande Valley and Lima regions. Students from any college or department will be selected to work in bi-national multidisciplinary teams to develop technological products to address a regional need (e.g. access to clean water, home technologies, etc.). In the first part of the program UNI students will visit UTRGV and then UTRGV students will visit UNI. The teams will receive training and support for their specific projects in a variety of relevant topics such as engineering design, sociocultural considerations, and business modeling. This will be complemented with site visits (e.g. local industry, research centers, etc.), guest presentations (e.g. government officials, NGO representatives, etc.) and sociocultural experiences (e.g. visits to Machu Picchu, Lima’s colonial sites, etc.). At the end of the program, the students will present their solutions to a “shark tank” of academicians, community representatives and entrepreneurs. Each team must apply for a patent and also learn the process of submitting their product to a regional or national student innovation funding competition. Our objective is to engage the UTRGV and UNI student communities by learning from each other and creating a culture of innovation where anyone can tackle a real problem and file a patent. We will train our students as resilient innovators to overcome scarcity of resources through creativity and resourcefulness. This will be achieved by providing a non-traditional learning environment outside the classroom where students apply STEAM knowledge to develop technical and professional skills by working on a real problem. The RGV and Lima innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem is emerging and our regions face multiple similar challenges. Our regions will benefit from these resilient innovators and their leadership will create opportunities to improve the quality of life of the RGV, Lima and beyond. If funded, this would be the first study abroad program originating from the College of Engineering and Computer Scienc e and the first extramurally funded study abroad program at UTRGV.

presentation.title: Improvement of laser-induced graphene-based electrochemical biosensors through graphene-conductive polymer ink coating for sensitive detection of alpha-fetoprotein
presentation.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common type of primary liver cancer and is the sixth most commonly occurring cancer worldwide with the second-highest mortality rate [1] [2]. Since the 1970s, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) has been used as a prominent biomarker for the diagnosis of HCC. But AFP is electrochemically inactive, thus, detecting AFP is unreliable for early detection of HCC [3]. In this study, we demonstrated the highly sensitive detection of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) by developing an electrochemical biosensor using Kapton film. The electrochemical sensor was fabricated by laser scribing technique which is a one-step method that does not require any oxidative acid synthesis route or chemical vapor deposition (CVD) to obtain graphene structure which reduced the cost tremendously [4]. The laser-induced graphene (LIG) electrodes were modified with developed graphene polyaniline (G-PANI) ink to effectively enhance the detection of electrical signals. The peak potential voltage difference was 600μV for the bare electrode, while after modifying with the ink the difference was reduced to 260 μV which indicates a 56% change. Therefore, the electrocatalytic effect of the electrode surface and electrochemical sensor signal was improved after modifying the electrode with ink. To evaluate the performance of the sensor, differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) techniques were performed in phosphate buffer saline (PBS) buffer with ferro-ferricyanide as the redox probe. For the DPV method, a significant surge in peak current was observed, increasing from 9.2 microamperes at a concentration of 20 pg/mL to 13.6 microamperes at 400 pg/mL which satisfied the fact that increasing the concentration of AFP, led to a higher number of analytes available for electron transfer, thus resulting in the observed current enhancement. The nearly identical current outputs in the DPV measurements were obtained consecutive 15 times which represents the sensor’s stability with an RSD of 3.69% and exhibits high reproducibility (RSD=12.15%, N=5). The obtained EIS result showed good linearity in charge transfer resistance change (coefficient of determination, R2= 0.87) with the AFP concentration increment in the range of 20 pg/mL - 400 pg/mL, and the limit of detection (LOD) was 146 pg/mL at a signal-to-noise ratio of 3, indicating the sensor's sensitivity. The range was selected due to demonstrate high sensitivity in the picogram range and has the potential to cover the entire physiological range for a healthy adult. The specific selectivity of the sensor was evidenced by obtaining a random current peak when both AFP and estrogen were introduced simultaneously on the surface of the sensor. For both electrochemical techniques, a similar coefficient of determination was found from the calibration curves, suggesting that the fabricated biosensor offers high selectivity to the determination of AFP biomarker.

presentation.title: The Art of Collaboration: Conflict Deactivation Protocols
presentation.abstract: The objective of this session is to share our experiences facing the additional challenges brought by multidisciplinary collaboration and offer the audience a “toolkit” of basic solutions when conflicts appear. Real-life challenges require multidisciplinary teams collaborating to generate comprehensive solutions, but collaborating across disciplines can be challenging. The authors come from three different fields with the objective of tackling food security challenges (UN Sustainable Development Goal #2: zero hunger). Dr. Vargas is an expert on innovative product design, Dr. Robles is an expert on business entrepreneurship, and Dr. Robles is an expert on agriculture and life sciences. The team has been collaborating for over 5 years with students working on hands-on projects. Looking back, we are proud of our work with the students, but it has been a learning process. Abbreviated session description Multidisciplinary collaboration is necessary to provide comprehensive solutions for real-life problems, but it can be challenging. In this session the authors present a conflict resolution toolkit based on 5 years of multidisciplinary collaboration tackling food security challenges. Key takeaways/goals for your session Tips on how to tackle conflicts in multidisciplinary collaboration.

presentation.title: Training Students to Self-Transform: Applying Design Thinking for Freshmen Academic Success
presentation.abstract: Freshman engineering students can have a hard time transitioning to college. The freshman year is critical to the students’ academic success; in this year they learn basic skills and establish essential networks with other students, faculty, and resources. How can we help these freshman engineering students in this transition? In this seminar, Dr. Noe Vargas Hernandez will present a novel approach based on design thinking to train students to self-transform every time they face an academic and career path challenge. The premise is simple, engineering students learn about engineering design, technical creativity, and product innovation, what if they draw lessons by analogy to apply this knowledge to solve their academic challenges and to plan their professional career. In this case the students are themselves the product to design and redesign at every challenge in a process of continuous self-innovation. This work is funded by NSF award 2225247.

presentation.abstract: Real-life challenges, such as food security (giving the world access to sufficient food), demand comprehensive, sustainable solutions. Dr. Rampersad, a scientist, Dr. Robles, an entrepreneur, and Dr. Vargas, an engineer, decided 5 years ago to offer their students authentic learning experiences that prepare them to face these real-life challenges. However, this multidisciplinary collaboration has been painstakingly built step by step. In this talk, the speakers tell the story of this unique collaboration, the beginnings, challenges, ups and downs, and their practical “rules of engagement” that makes this an exemplary multidisciplinary sustainable collaboration. The collaboration model can be theoretically represented with multiple interconnected helices (biology, engineering, entrepreneurship, society, etc.), but in practical terms it can be simply summarized as “we are one team”.

presentation.title: Webinar: Catalyzing Sustainable Innovation and Entrepreneurship in Higher Education Ecosystems
presentation.organization: The Association for the Advancement of Sustainability in Higher Education
presentation.abstract: According to a recent Nielsen study, ~54% of Gen Z want to be entrepreneurs. Colleges and universities have taken note and are proactively tailoring their program offerings to meet the increased demand for entrepreneurial training and education. Entrepreneurship is a powerful force that fosters innovation and creates the goods and services through which we work, play, and experience life. It is the engine that drives these mediums to be more affordable, more efficient, and more impactful, which, in theory, should lead to a better quality of life. However, if left unregulated, entrepreneurial growth can have negative consequences on certain segments of our population and the environment. Hence, a better model of innovation and entrepreneurship needs to be adopted–one that balances growth, inclusion, and sustainability and doesn’t frame them as trade-offs. Are these components mutually exclusive or can they be simultaneously prioritized? In this webinar, we’ll discuss the significance of sustainable innovation and entrepreneurship and explore the ways that growth, inclusion, and sustainability are connected through an exercise using a sustainable business model canvas.

presentation.title: Characterization of vegetable oil-based lubricants with Halloysite Nanotubes as lubricant additives and their tribological performance
presentation.event: 16th North American Conference on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management
presentation.abstract: Vegetable oil-based nano-lubricants are a great alternative to petroleum-based lubricants due to their less adverse impact on the environment. This work evaluated the tribological performance of sunflower, corn, and peanut oils with the addition of Halloysite Nanotubes (HNT) as lubricant additives at different concentrations. Vegetable oils are commercially used as edible oils, but in this current work they were selected as base oils for the nano-lubricants due to their renewability and biodegradability. To analyze the tribology performance of the nano-lubricants, a block-on-ring tribometer was used following the ASTM G-077-05 standard procedure. In addition, tapping torque tests were carried out following the ASTM D5619 standard. Results indicated that sunflower, corn, and peanut oils mixed with HNT at 1.5 wt% provided the best tribological performance. The wear volume loss was lowered by 29%, 78%, and 67% for sunflower, corn, and peanut oil respectively, with the addition of 1.5 wt%, compared to its base oil. Tapping torque test results also provided high tapping torque efficiency that can prolong tool life in machining processes. Based on the experimental results, it can be concluded that the vegetable oils modified with the addition of halloysite nano-clay have the potential to be used as biodegradable lubricants.

presentation.title: Development and Characterization of Cold Spray Coatings for Aerospace and Defense Manufacturing
presentation.event: 16th North American Conference on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management
presentation.abstract: Cold Spray is a type of thermal metal spraying which uses heated gas/air to propel metal powder onto the surface of a substrate to create a coating or repair damaged or corroded metal components. The powder feedstock materials are spherical gas atomized metal powders ranging in size from 20-50 microns in diameter for best results. Cold spray systems use low temperatures ranging from 200-900 °C compared to existing additive manufacturing methods which use much higher temperatures to melt metal. These lower heating temperatures only semi-melt the metal powder particles allowing for them to undergo plastic deformation as they are deposited onto the surface of the substrate. The main objective of this project is to develop and characterize cold spray coatings using aluminum, copper, and nickel powders deposited on different substrates varying processing parameters. As cold spray can be used in different coating applications with a wide range of different metals and alloys, coatings have an unlimited range in applications where rapid repair and high-quality coatings are needed. The ease of use of this technology has a promising future in aerospace and defense applications as it provides a low-cost solution in corrosion prevention and repair of damaged components.

presentation.title: Development of Grapeseed oil-based nanolubricants using TiO2 nanoparticles as lubricant additives
presentation.abstract: Recently, there has been growing concern regarding the use of petroleum-based lubricants. This concern has caused interest in readily biodegradable lubricants such as vegetable oils. The present study evaluates the lubrication performance of grapeseed oil modified with varying titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ) nanoparticles of sizes 5, 18 and 40 nanometers as lubricant additives at different concentrations. The wear protection and friction characteristics of the oil-formulations were evaluated by means of block-on-ring sliding tests following the ASTM G-077-05 standard procedure. The experimental set up consisted in an AISI 52100 bearing steel alloy test ring rotating against an AISI 304 stainless steel block. During the sliding wear tests, nano-lubricants were placed in an oil bath chamber to allow constant lubrication, while the test ring rotated, covering it in lubricant by the action of centrifugal forces. The experimental results showed that the coefficient of friction decreased when adding 5, 18, and 40 nanometer particles by 83.95%, 62.82%, and 77.50% respectively. Furthermore, the volume loss was lowered by 77.80%, 82.19%, and 78.77% with the addition of the 5, 18, and 40 nanometer TiO 2 nanoparticles, respectively. Based on the experimental results it is concluded that modified grapeseed with the addition of different sized nanoparticles has the potential for use as a biodegradable lubricant. Additionally, this improvement in the lubrication could provide a longer life to machines with moving parts that require the use of lubricants, resulting in lower costs.

presentation.title: Development of Vegetable Oil-based Nano-lubricants using MMT Nanoparticles as Lubricant Additives
presentation.event: 16th North American Conference on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management
presentation.abstract: Because of the environmental impact and price volatility, there has been a growing concern on the use of petroleum-based lubricants. This issue has stimulated research into the development of biodegradable lubricants like vegetable oils. In this study, the tribological and rheological behavior of sunflower, peanut, and corn oils modified with montmorillonite nanoclay (MMT) as lubricant additives were evaluated at various concentrations. A custom-made block on ring tribotester was used to evaluate the wear and friction characteristics of the nano-lubricants, following the ASTM G-077-05 standard. The effects of concentration and shear rate on shear viscosity were studied using a parallel plate rheometer, and the experimental data was compared with conventional models. Analytical methods, including scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-Ray diffraction (XRD), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and profilometry, were used to characterize the morphology and structure of the MMT nanoclay, as well as the worn surfaces. The experimental results showed that the volumetric wear and coefficient of friction decreased with the addition of MMT nanoparticles, at different concentrations, compared to the base vegetable oils. In conclusion, the newly developed vegetable oil-based nano-lubricants with the addition of MMT nanoclay, look like a promising environmentally friendly solution to compete with petroleum-based lubricants.

If I Can Measure It, I Can Improve It: Teaching Design & Innovation Experiences to Undergraduate Students
presentation.abstract: Organizations (such as the d.School, KEEN, and VentureWell) have laid major groundwork in making design thinking educational resources more accessible to educators across campus and throughout the nation. As a result, engineering programs are integrating design opportunities outside of the traditional freshman introductory engineering courses and senior design capstone. Many engineering programs have developed design spines, where engineering students get to experience design throughout the typical four-year experience. Moreover, many engineering educators are starting to integrate design experiences in the mid-level fundamental courses as a way to connect theoretical concepts to real-world learning. Although design and innovation opportunities have come a long way for engineering students, there is still much to be done with respect to the development and offering of evaluation and assessment resources for engineering educators. There is a variety of approaches for evaluating and assessing design and innovation experiences, each with a different perspective. Understanding these different approaches is helpful to effectively measure the impact of design and innovation learning experiences and for continuous improvement. The purpose of this poster session is to showcase a “backwards curriculum design” holistic focused toolbox which summarizes the various learning evaluation approaches as it aligns to the learning activity and learning objective. Evaluation categories include the following: (1) Process, (2) Product/Outcome, (3) Integration of Engineering Fundamentals, (4) Constraint Focus, (5) Teamwork, and (6) Communication.

Wearable Prophylaxis for the Prevention of Deep Vein Thrombosis in Patients of Post-Op Hip/ Knee Surgery
presentation.organization: UTRGV College of Engineering and Computer Science
presentation.abstract: For patients in post-operation of hip and knee surgery, there is an increased risk of blood clots forming due to poor blood circulation. The lack of sufficient blood flow is due to reduced stimulation in the calf muscle and lack of lower leg exercise in general. Because of the possibility of blood clots forming in the deep venous systems of these patients, they are at large risk of Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and subsequently death from a Pulmonary Embolism (PE). Current solutions for DVT prevention in outpatients have many drawbacks, and a more effective and less expensive solution is desired. There is a product opportunity gap for a device which would fulfill these needs in a user-friendly and affordable manner. In this work, we propose a wearable mechanical “boot” which would aid in creating the blood flow necessary for DVT prevention. The proposed solution will increase user compliance and be a more effective means of blood flow creation while being marketable to places such as hospital purchase committees. A market study and design for manufacturability are considered in generating prototypes. The end goal is progress towards a device which will become a real product.

presentation.title: Assessing the lubrication performance of SiO2 and TiO2 nanoparticles as lubricant additives on grapeseed oil
presentation.abstract: Recently, there has been growing concern regarding the use of petroleum-based lubricants. This concern has caused interest in readily biodegradable lubricants such as vegetable oils. The present study evaluates the lubrication performance of grapeseed oil modified with silicon dioxide (SiO 2 ) and titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ) nanoparticles as lubricant additives at different concentrations. The wear protection and friction characteristics of the oil-formulations were evaluated by means of block-on-ring sliding tests following the ASTM G-077-05 standard procedure. The experimental set up consisted in an AISI 52100 bearing steel alloy test ring rotating against an AISI 304 stainless steel block. During the sliding wear tests, nano-lubricants were placed in an oil bath chamber to allow constant lubrication, while the test ring rotated, covering it in lubricant by the action of centrifugal forces. The experimental results showed that the coefficient of friction decreased with the addition of SiO 2 and TiO 2 nanoparticles by 49.7% and 62.8%, respectively when compared to grapeseed oil without nanoparticle additives. In addition, the volume loss was lowered by 38.6% and 82.2%, with the addition of SiO 2 and TiO 2 nanoparticles, respectively. Based on the experimental results, it was concluded that modified grapeseed oil enhanced with nanoparticles has the potential for use as a good biodegradable lubricant. Additionally, this improvement in the lubrication could provide a longer life to machines with moving parts that require the use of lubricants, resulting in lower costs.

presentation.title: Design and development of a Pin-on-Disc tribometer for testing under extreme-pressures
presentation.abstract: Tribotester is the general name given to a machine or device used to perform tests and simulations of wear, friction and lubrication which are the subject of the study of tribology. Tribological conditions in bulk metal forming processes are characterized by high contact pressures and large relative movements at high velocities between the tool and the workpiece. The present project is focused in the design and build of a pin-on-disc tribometer device capable to perform tribological tests under extreme-pressure conditions and to measure the wear and the coefficient of friction (COF) for a pair of materials, depending on the presence and kind of a lubricant, sliding velocity, and applied load. The pin-on-disc tribometer design consists in a drive system, a control system, a test chamber, a load arm, an extreme-load arm, a force sensor, and software for measurements and data acquisition. The tribosystem comprises a stationary pin (or ball) pressed at the required load against the disc rotating at the defined speed. The friction couple will be inserted in a test chamber. During the tests the following quantities will be measured: friction force, chamber temperature, rotational speed, and the number of disc revolutions (sliding distance). Technical specifications of the tribotester will be: nominal ball diameter of 9.525 mm, nominal disc diameter of 28.575 mm, sliding speed up to 500 rpm, and normal load up to 400 N. With the development of the proposed equipment, tribological tests could be conducted in accordance with the ASTM G99 standard.

presentation.title: Development of a new testing device to evaluate the durability of biocompatible materials and reach out RGV students within the STEM fields.
presentation.abstract: One of the main causes of hip prostheses failure is the premature wear of their components. Multi-directional motion or “cross-shear” motion has been identified as one of the most significant factors affecting the wear rate of UHMWPE in total hip joint replacement prostheses. To better evaluate the effect of this cross-shear motion on the tribological behavior of different biomaterials, a new wear testing device has been designed and developed. This new instrument is capable to reproduce the “cross-shear” effect with bidirectional motion on bearing materials and to determine coefficient of friction (COF) between surfaces during testing. To validate the functionality of this new testing platform, alumina balls were articulated against Ti-6Al-4V ELI alloy disks in Ringer’s solution. Four different articulation patterns, all with identical path lengths per cycle, were tested. Gravimetric weight loss was converted to volumetric wear data in order to determine the effects of motion patterns on the wear. Worn surfaces were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy. This scientific approach to quantifying the tribological effects of cross-shear provides fundamental data that are crucial in evaluating potential biomaterials for use in knee and hip joint replacements. In addition, the development of this new testing device will facilitate efforts at UTRGV to reach out students from traditionally under-represented groups within the science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields.

presentation.title: Development of biodegradable nano-lubricants using coconut oil modified with nanoparticles as lubricant additives at UTRGV
presentation.abstract: In metal-forming processes, the use of lubricants for providing desirable tribological conditions at tool-workpiece interface is critical to increase the material formability and prolonging tool life. Nowadays, the depletion of crude oil reserves in the world and the global concern in protecting the environment from contamination have renewed interest in developing environment friendly lubricants derived from alternative sources such as vegetable oils. In the present study, the rheological and tribological behavior of coconut oil modified with nanoparticle additives was experimentally evaluated. Two different nanoparticle additives were investigated: silicon dioxide (SiO 2 ), and copper oxide (CuO). For the two conditions, nanoparticles were dispersed at different concentrations within the coconut oil. The effects of concentration and shear rate on the viscosity were evaluated and the experimental data was compared with conventional models. A custom made tribotester was used to evaluate the effect of concentration on the tribological performance of the nano-lubricants. The experimental results showed that wear volume loss was lowered by 37% and 33% using SiO 2 and CuO nanoparticles respectively. Furthermore, the addition of SiO 2 and CuO nanoparticles decreased the coefficient of friction (COF) by 93.75% and 93.25% respectively as compared to coconut oil without nanoparticles. In addition, nano-lubrication projects at UTRGV will act as a vehicle to expose more UTRGV students to scientific research, to provide them with more opportunities to publish in scientific journals and present their work at symposiums, as well as to better prepare them to enter the STEM workforce and/or encourage them to pursue advanced degrees.

presentation.abstract: Nowadays, global concern on the pollution created by conventional mineral have renewed interest in developing environment friendly lubricants derived from alternative sources such as vegetable oils. In the present study, tribological and rheological performance of coconut oil modified with nanoparticle additives was experimentally evaluated. The lubricant wear and friction characteristics were found using cross-cylinder and block on ring configurations. Two different nanoparticle additives were investigated: silicon dioxide (SiO 2 ), and copper oxide (CuO). For the two conditions, nanoparticles were dispersed at different concentrations within the vegetable oil. Using a parallel plate rheometer, the rheological behavior for all the concentrations were analyzed. The experimental results showed that wear volume loss was lowered by 33% using both SiO 2 and CuO nanoparticles. Furthermore, the addition of SiO 2 and CuO nanoparticles decreased the coefficient of friction by 57% and 65% respectively as compared to coconut oil without nanoparticles. presentation.title: Micro-Texturing of UHMWPE to Increase the Longevity of Prosthetic Hip and Knee Replacements
presentation.abstract: After many years of repetitive stress and strain on human joints, bones start to break down and are in need of replacements. As a result, 1.25 million yearly joint surgeries are performed alone with the average patient age being 50-70 years old. Current methods allow for an average joint lifespan of ~7-15 years, which is influenced by complications such as excessive implant wear – one of the leading causes of joint dislocation and infection. As of today, joint replacements are made of smooth surfaced Ultra-High Molecular Weight Polyethylene (UHMWPE). It is believed that current methods help minimize wear rate, but novel studies suggest that micro-texturing the UHMWPE’s surface decreases wear rate even further increasing the longevity of the replacement. Surface textures allow for the collection of natural lubrication within themselves providing a cushioning effect against the adjacent joint. The texturing also serves as a pocket mechanism that collects joint-replacement debris keeping it from entering the bloodstream. Using a Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machine, a variety of polygonal geometries will be micro-machined onto the surface of the UHMWPE. Geometric parameters such polygon diameters, side lengths, shape spacing, and depth will be varied over multiple experimental runs to determine the optimal pattern configuration. Validation of the proposed pattern will be completed using a tribometer device with Ringer’s solution as lubricant. The gathered experimental data will then be analyzed in efforts to generate empirical models that will predict replacement longevity as a function of surface geometry.

presentation.title: Tribological Characterization of Vegetable Lubricants Reinforced with Halloysite Clay Nanotubes
presentation.organization: Society of Tribologists and Lubrication Engineers (STLE)
presentation.abstract: Manufacturing processes commonly use lubricants to decrease the friction between moving components, reducing vibration and improving the efficiency of the process. Usually these cutting fluids or lubricants are based on mineral oils and have additives which are not environmentally friendly, increasing the costs of the process from lubricant disposal. Therefore, there is an increasing need to employ environmentally friendly lubricants such as vegetable oils. Nanoparticles additives have also been studied in order to improve the tribological properties of these lubricants. In this study, lubricants of soy, corn, peanut and sunflower seed were additized with environmentally-friendly halloysite clay nanotubes in concentrations of0.01, 0.05, 0.10 wt.% by ultrasonication. Tribological properties were characterized under anti-wear and extreme-pressure conditions using a T-02 four-ball and a T-05 block-on-ring tribotesters. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of bio based nano-lubricants to be used in manufacturing processes.

presentation.title: Centrifugally Spun Carbon Composite Fibers and Their use as Anode Materials in Lithium-ion Batteries
presentation.abstract: We present results on the centrifugal spinning of Metal-oxides (MOx)/PAN and Metal-Sulfides (MS)/PAN precursors for the mass production of MOx /C and MS/C composite fibers as anode materials for Lithium-ion batteries. MOx and MS such as NiO, TiO2, and SnO2, SnS2 and MoS2 were chosen with carbon as the active materials for the composite-fibers anodes. The microfiber preparation process involved the centrifugal spinning of MOx/MS/PAN precursors into microfibers and subsequent stabilization in air at 280oC and calcination at 700oC under Argon atmosphere. The MOx/C and MS/C composite-fibers anodes exhibited a specific capacity between 300 and 1200 mAhg-1 at the first cycle with a high irreversible capacity. The initial high irreversible capacity was attributed to the formation of the SEI layer and the high surface area of the centrifugally spun composite microfibers. In the subsequent cycles, the MOx/C and MS/C composite-fibers anodes exhibited a much stable cycling performance, i.e. 150-600 mAhg-1 was maintained after 100 cycles. The effect of pre-lithiation of the electrode after the first discharge cycle and coating the composite fibers-anode with active materials, prior to cycling, was systematically investigated. The pre-lithiation of carbon composite-fibers anodes after the first cycle exhibited higher charge/discharge capacities and higher Coulombic efficiency up to 98% than the pristine carbon composite fibers

Impact of silicate contaminants on tribological and thermal transport performance of greases
presentation.event: 22nd International Conference on Wear of Materials (WOM)
presentation.abstract: This work investigates the effects on thermal transport and tribological performance of incorporating silicate particles - emulating pollutants - within various greases: lithium thickened(MB), soap complex thickened (SB) and silica thickened (UB). Silicate particles (200-300 μm)were homogeneously dispersed, by a mechanical method, within the selected greases in concentrations of 1.5g/10 ml. For tribological evaluation a four-ball tribotester was employed according to ASTM D2266 standard test method for wear preventive characteristics of lubricating greases. For the silica thickened grease (UB) the WSD increased by 60%; for the lithium soap and the complex soap thickened greases, the changes were almost negligible due to the behavior of their soap thickener and base oil. For the thermal transport evaluation, a guarded hot-plate method-based apparatus was used to characterize the thermal conductivity of greases with and without silicate particles, showing an enhancement range of 25 - 70% in thermal conductivity with the addition of 1.5g/10 ml of silicate particles. Thermal conductivity measurements offer an accuracy of ~ 5%. It was shown that MB and SB greases have a positive impact on the thermal conductivity as silicates are added; UB reflected a negative effect on the thermal conductivity as silicates were mixed within the grease. These results show that silicate contaminants may be able to thermal properties of greases while not affecting significantly their tribological performance.

NUMERICAL SIMULATION OF WAVE ENERGY CONVERTER WITH HYDROFOIL BLADES UNDER VARIOUS WAVE CONDITIONS
presentation.event: ASME 2019 13th International Conference on Energy Sustainability
presentation.abstract: Ocean wave is a rich source of renewable energy with much higher power density than winds. Various WEC technologies have been proposed or are under development. In this study, we developed a 2-dimensional (2D) model and analyzed the rotational motion of the lift-type rotor’s blade under steady flow and unsteady flow. The numerical model was validated by experiments under steady flow. Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) analysis was performed to identify the major contribution of frequency in terms of vortexes generated in the flow field. A comparative study was also performed by comparing all the cases in terms of energy conversion efficiency under different wave conditions. It turns out that the efficiency of energy conversion has a maximum value in the steady flow, while the efficiency for unsteady flow keeps decreasing, therefore this is highly due to the increased dissipation because of the oscillating. When the flow is oscillating, the rotational speed of the rotor under periodic condition is lower than the rotational velocity with steady flow, and a curve fitting was performed in this study to predict the periodic average rotational speed. We conclude that for oscillating flow a minimum of 1.6% energy conversion efficiency can be expected, but it may vary for the actual ocean waves. It is expected the current 2D simulation results can contribute to the wave energy community, especially when the rotor design and optimization is required.

presentation.title: The Effect of Metal-Oxide Coating on the Electrochemical Performance of Carbon-Nanofibers Anodes in Lithium-ion Batteries
presentation.abstract: With the invention of the electric cars and the exponential growth in portable electronics over the last decade, energy storage systems that can supply and store more power are of utmost importance. Li-ion batteries (LIBs) entered the market less than a decade ago to keep up with market demands and have since become the most efficient way to store energy due to their reversible nature. Graphite is currently the most widely used material in (LIB) anodes due to its long cycle life and low manufacturing cost, its main drawback being its low theoretical capacity of 372 mAg-1. Metal oxides have been of interest as electrode materials for (LIBs) due to their inherently high theoretical capacities and low cost. However, the main drawback of metal oxide-based anodes includes high volume expansion, particle agglomeration, and dendrite formation. Developments in composites and novel micro/nano-structures that withstand large temperature ranges and maintain structural stability have attracted interest for their use as electrode materials in LIBs. Here, we explore the performance of Iron Oxide (Fe2O3), Tin Oxide (SnO2), Zinc Oxide (ZnO), and Cobalt Oxide (Co3O4), coated on carbon fibers as hosts for lithium ion insertion/de-insertion during charge/discharge process. The synthesis and design of Fe2O3/Carbon and SnO2/C composite fibers were reiliazed by the centrifugal spinning of metal-oxides precursors in polyacrylonitrile (PAN)/ dimethylformamide (DMF) solutions and followed by calcination at 600 °C in an inert gas. The characterization of Fe2O3/C, ZnO/C, Co3O4/C and SnO2/C composite fibers was conducted using X-Ray Diffraction (XRD), Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive X-ray analysis (EDAX). The pre-coated carbon fibers with metal-oxide nanoparticle precursors showed improved electrochemical performance compared to the pristine composite carbon-fibers anodes.

presentation.title: A Hybridized Approach to STEM Laboratories
presentation.event: Sparking Innovation in Online and Hybrid Learning
presentation.organization: Center for Online Learning and Teaching Technology
presentation.abstract: he foundation of engineering laboratories is always to provide a chance to understand and explore theoretical concepts presented in lecture. Unfortunately, most students lack the understanding of the concepts to fully understand the hands-on activities that labs provide. The session will present a possible solution that introduces students to a pre-laboratory hybridized approach. Students are able to explore SoftChalk lectures to understand both procedures and theoretical background behind the laboratory work – the lecture will check for understanding and provide them a grade for their work. Additionally, a laboratory manual is provided where they have access to guidance to each of their labs. In order determine if the students have read their lab procedures, quizzing is done 10 minutes before lab. The quizzes provide automated feedback that is valuable to the students and instructor. Additionally, most of the labs introduced in materials engineering involve high-powered, expensive, rotating equipment. Safety is a primary concern. To introduce the students to their equipment, safety operating procedure (SOP) videos add a new level of interest and investment to both the lab and the hybrid environment.

presentation.title: Design and Development of an Independently Operated Aesthetic Falling Aid Device for Physically Disabled People
presentation.event: UTRGV School of Medicine Inaugural Research Symposium
presentation.abstract: The present investigation is about a self-operated fall aid device. The main objective of this investigation was the development of a fall aid device with the functionality of being operated by the affected person without the need for external help. The secondary objective was to achieve a simple design with a low cost and capable of hiding in plain sight. The developed fall aid device provides a physically impaired person the ease of achieving a seated position after falling to the floor. The device is easily operated by solely the affected person. The apparatus includes a rigid frame divided into three sections to adapt to the human body in a seated position after the device has transformed. This structure provides a solid support to maintain the person seated. The lifting device includes a pump to inflate a set of inflatable chambers. This set of chambers is located below the middle section of the frame that act as the lifting mechanism of the apparatus. As previously mentioned, one of the main features of the device is its simple design and ability to be hidden in plain sight. This was done by disguising it as a rug that can be placed anywhere in a room. The method used to develop this investigation was the observation of similar product to achieve the objective of helping a disabled person to be lifted from the ground.

presentation.title: Impact of the ADVANCE Women of Color Summer Writing Retreat at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, a Hispanic-Serving Institution
presentation.event: NSF ADVANCE/GSE Program Workshop Broadening Participation: Intersectionality
presentation.abstract: Seven minority-serving institutions led by Jackson State University launched the ADVANCE Women of Color Summer Writing Retreat (SWR) for women faculty to build multi-institutional networks of collaborators and complete a writing project. The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) was the sole Hispanic-serving institution in the consortium and hosted the summer writing retreat in May 2016 with 16 participants; 25 percent were faculty of color. Participants were from traditional science disciplines, social and behavioral sciences, engineering, and information systems. The SWR experience included pre-retreat work, one week in-residence, and post-retreat online accountability coaching. Results of the SWR included the completion and submission of seven grant proposals and ten manuscripts. Importantly, the retreat provided a forum for women faculty in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) to experience an intensive writing program with one-on-one coaching, online coaching, and networking. UTRGV has established an in-house Summer Writing Program and Faculty Writing Program that utilize many best practices (e.g., coaching, networking, and accountability) from the SWR. Furthermore, UTRGV plans to offer another writing retreat in 2018. The institutionalization of writing programs is important in the development and retention of women faculty in STEM at UTRGV, especially as the institution becomes more research-focused.
